1.name: hydrogen
1.description: Hydrogen is a chemical element with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the lightest and most abundant chemical element in the universe, constituting about 75% of all normal matter. Under standard conditions, hydrogen is a gas of diatomic molecules with the formula H2, called dihydrogen, which is colorless, odorless, non-toxic, and highly combustible.
1.uses: Hydrogen's main industrial uses include fossil fuel processing and ammonia production for fertilizer. It is also used in nuclear fusion, as a tracer in isotope geochemistry, and in specialized self-powered lighting devices. Emerging uses for hydrogen include the use of fuel cells to generate electricity.
1.characteristics: Dihydrogen is colorless, odorless, non-toxic, and highly flammable, reacting with oxygen to produce liquid water and releasing 286 kilojoules of heat per mole. Hydrogen gas forms explosive mixtures with air in concentrations from 4% to 74% and has an autoignition temperature of 500 °C. Hydrogen flames emit faint blue and ultraviolet light.

2.name: helium
2.description: Helium is a colorless, odorless, non-toxic, inert, monatomic gas and the first in the noble gas group in the periodic table. It has symbol He and atomic number 2. It is the second-lightest and second-most abundant element in the observable universe, after hydrogen.
2.uses: Liquid helium is used in cryogenics and in the cooling of superconducting magnets, with its main commercial application in MRI scanners. Other industrial uses include as a pressurizing and purge gas, as a protective atmosphere for arc welding, and in crystal growing processes. It is also used as a lifting gas in balloons and airships, and is important in scientific research for studying quantum mechanics and phenomena near absolute zero.
2.characteristics: Helium has the lowest boiling point among all elements and does not have a melting point at standard pressures. It is colorless and odorless, and helium-4 exhibits superfluidity at temperatures near absolute zero. Terrestrial helium is relatively rare at 5.2 ppm by volume in the atmosphere, but can be concentrated in natural gas fields in concentrations as great as 7% by volume.

3.name: lithium
3.description: Lithium is a chemical element with symbol Li and atomic number 3. It is a soft, silvery-white alkali metal that under standard conditions is the least dense metal and the least dense solid element. Like all alkali metals, lithium is highly reactive and flammable, and must be stored in vacuum, inert atmosphere, or inert liquid.
3.uses: Lithium and its compounds have several industrial applications including heat-resistant glass and ceramics, lithium grease lubricants, flux additives for iron, steel and aluminium production, and lithium metal and lithium-ion batteries, which alone consume more than three-quarters of lithium production. Lithium-based drugs are useful as a mood stabilizer and antidepressant in the treatment of mental illness such as bipolar disorder. Lithium metal is often used in coolants for heat transfer applications due to its high specific heat capacity.
3.characteristics: Lithium is soft enough to be cut with a knife and has a silvery-white appearance that oxidizes to lithium oxide in air. It has the lowest density of all metals at 0.534 g/cm³ and can float on water and light hydrocarbon oils. Its melting point is 180.50°C and boiling point is 1,342°C, both the highest of all alkali metals, and it has a mass specific heat capacity of 3.58 kilojoules per kilogram-kelvin, the highest of all solids.

4.name: beryllium
4.description: Beryllium is a chemical element with symbol Be and atomic number 4. It is a steel-gray, hard, strong, lightweight and brittle alkaline earth metal that occurs naturally only in combination with other elements to form minerals. It is relatively rare in the universe, usually occurring as a product of the spallation of larger atomic nuclei that have collided with cosmic rays.
4.uses: In structural applications, beryllium is used for aircraft components, missiles, spacecraft, and satellites due to its high flexural rigidity, thermal stability, and low density. It is the most common window material for X-ray equipment and particle detectors because of its transparency to X-rays and ionizing radiation. When added as an alloying element to aluminum, copper, iron, or nickel, beryllium improves physical properties, and beryllium copper alloys are used to make tools and components that are strong and do not create sparks.
4.characteristics: Beryllium is steel gray and brittle at room temperature with a close-packed hexagonal crystal structure and exceptional stiffness (Young's modulus 287 GPa). It has a melting point of 1287 °C and a low density of 1.85 times that of water, with the highest sound conduction speed among metals at about 12.9 km/s. It dissipates the most heat per unit weight among all metals and has a relatively low coefficient of linear thermal expansion, making it uniquely stable under extreme temperature differences.

5.name: boron
5.description: Boron is a chemical element with symbol B and atomic number 5. In its crystalline form it is a brittle, dark, lustrous metalloid; in its amorphous form it is a brown powder. As the lightest element of the boron group it has three valence electrons for forming covalent bonds.
5.uses: The primary use of elemental boron is as boron filaments in high-strength materials. Boron is primarily used in chemical compounds, with about half of all production consumed globally as an additive in fiberglass for insulation and structural materials. It is also used in polymers and ceramics for high-strength, lightweight structural and heat-resistant materials, in borosilicate glass, as sodium perborate for bleaching, as a dopant in semiconductors, and in some boron-containing organic pharmaceuticals.
5.characteristics: Crystalline boron is silvery to black, extremely hard at 9.3 on the Mohs scale, and a poor electrical conductor at room temperature with electrical conductivity of 1.5 × 10−6 Ω−1 cm−1. It has a melting point above 2000 °C and is chemically inert and resistant to attack by boiling hydrofluoric or hydrochloric acid. Natural boron is composed of two stable isotopes: boron-11 (80.1%) and boron-10 (19.9%).

6.name: carbon
6.description: Carbon is a nonmetallic chemical element with symbol C and atomic number 6. It is tetravalent, able to form up to four covalent bonds due to having 4 valence electrons, and belongs to group 14 of the periodic table. It is the 15th most abundant element in Earth's crust and the fourth most abundant in the universe by mass after hydrogen, helium, and oxygen.
6.uses: Carbon serves as the common element of all known life due to its abundance, unique diversity of organic compounds, and unusual ability to form polymers at temperatures commonly encountered on Earth. It is used in the iron and steel industry in smelting reactions and to control carbon content of steel. Carbon forms metallic carbides like tungsten carbide that are used as abrasives and for making hard tips for cutting tools, and graphene could potentially be used in space elevator construction and to store hydrogen for hydrogen-based engines.
6.characteristics: Carbon atoms can bond together in diverse ways resulting in various allotropes including graphite, diamond, amorphous carbon, and fullerenes. The physical properties vary widely: graphite is opaque, black, and soft enough to write with, while diamond is highly transparent and the hardest naturally occurring material. Graphite conducts electricity while diamond has low electrical conductivity, and under normal conditions diamond, carbon nanotubes, and graphene have the highest thermal conductivities of all known materials. Carbon has the highest sublimation point of all elements and is chemically resistant, resisting all but the strongest oxidizers at standard temperature and pressure.

7.name: nitrogen
7.description: Nitrogen is a chemical element with symbol N and atomic number 7. It is a nonmetal and the lightest member of group 15 of the periodic table. At standard temperature and pressure, two atoms bond to form N2, a colorless and odorless diatomic gas that comprises about 78% of Earth's atmosphere.
7.uses: Elemental nitrogen is used as an inert gas for commercial uses such as food packaging and as liquid nitrogen in cryogenic applications. Many industrially important compounds containing nitrogen, such as ammonia, nitric acid, and organic nitrates, are used as propellants and explosives. Synthetically produced ammonia and nitrates serve as key industrial fertilizers, while nitrogen is also a constituent of organic compounds used in high-strength fabrics and superglue. Nitrogen is a constituent of every major pharmacological drug class, including antibiotics.
7.characteristics: Nitrogen has one of the highest electronegativities among elements at 3.04 on the Pauling scale. The element features an extremely strong triple bond in its elemental form (N≡N), which is the second strongest bond in any diatomic molecule after carbon monoxide. Nitrogen has a melting point of −210 °C and a boiling point of −196 °C, much lower than the rest of its group due to weak van der Waals interactions between N2 molecules.

8.name: oxygen
8.description: Oxygen is a chemical element with symbol O and atomic number 8, belonging to the chalcogen group in the periodic table. It is highly reactive, a nonmetal, and a potent oxidizing agent that readily forms oxides with most elements and compounds. At standard temperature and pressure, two oxygen atoms bind covalently to form dioxygen, a colorless and odorless diatomic gas that constitutes approximately 20.95% of Earth's atmosphere.
8.uses: Common industrial uses of oxygen include production of steel, plastics and textiles, brazing, welding and cutting of steels and other metals, rocket propellant, oxygen therapy, and life-support systems in aircraft, submarines, spaceflight, and diving. All eukaryotic organisms need oxygen for cellular respiration, a process that extracts chemical energy by the reaction of oxygen with organic molecules and releases carbon dioxide as a waste product.
8.characteristics: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust and the third-most abundant element in the universe after hydrogen and helium. It is highly reactive and does not remain as a free element in air without continuous replenishment through photosynthesis. The rarer allotrope ozone (O3) strongly absorbs UVB and UVC wavelengths and forms a protective layer in the lower stratosphere, though surface ozone is a corrosive air pollutant.

9.name: fluorine
9.description: Fluorine is a chemical element with symbol F and atomic number 9. It is the lightest halogen and exists at standard conditions as a pale yellow diatomic gas. Fluorine is extremely reactive, reacting with all other elements except for the light noble gases, and is highly toxic in its elemental form.
9.uses: Industrial production of fluorine gas is primarily used for uranium enrichment. Most commercial applications use fluorine compounds rather than pure fluorine, with about half of mined fluorite used in steelmaking and the rest converted into hydrogen fluoride or cryolite for aluminium refining. Organofluorine compounds are widely used as refrigerants, electrical insulation, PTFE (Teflon), and in pharmaceuticals, while the fluoride ion is used in toothpaste and water fluoridation to inhibit dental cavities.
9.characteristics: Fluorine atoms have nine electrons with configuration 1s²2s²2p⁵ and the highest electronegativity of any reactive element. The bond energy of difluorine is much lower than that of chlorine or bromine, accounting for its easy dissociation and high reactivity. At room temperature it is a pale yellow gas with a characteristic pungent odor, condenses into a bright yellow liquid at −188 °C, and has two solid forms (α- and β-fluorine) with different crystal structures.

10.name: neon
10.description: Neon is a chemical element with symbol Ne and atomic number 10, the second noble gas in the periodic table. It is a colorless, odorless, inert monatomic gas under standard conditions with approximately two-thirds the density of air. Neon was discovered in 1898 by British chemists William Ramsay and Morris Travers.
10.uses: Neon is used in low-voltage neon glow lamps, high-voltage discharge tubes, and neon advertising signs where it emits a distinct reddish-orange glow. The same red emission line is responsible for the characteristic red light of helium-neon lasers. Although neon has some applications in plasma tubes and as a refrigerant, its commercial uses are relatively limited.
10.characteristics: Neon is the second-lightest noble gas and is colorless and odorless. It glows reddish-orange in a vacuum discharge tube and has over 40 times the refrigerating capacity per unit volume of liquid helium and three times that of liquid hydrogen. Despite helium surpassing neon in ionization energy, neon is theorized to be the chemically least reactive of all elements, with no stable neutral or covalent neon compounds known to exist under any pressure or temperature.

11.name: sodium
11.description: Sodium is a chemical element with symbol Na and atomic number 11. It is a soft, silvery-white, highly reactive metal and an alkali metal in group 1 of the periodic table. Its only stable isotope is 23Na, and the free metal does not occur in nature but must be prepared from compounds.
11.uses: Sodium compounds have immense commercial importance in industries producing glass, paper, soap, and textiles. Sodium hydroxide (lye) is used in soap manufacture, and sodium chloride (edible salt) serves as a de-icing agent and nutrient for animals including humans. Sodium is essential for all animals and some plants, playing a major role in maintaining extracellular fluid osmotic pressure and enabling nerve impulse transmission through the action potential.
11.characteristics: Sodium is a soft silvery metal at standard temperature and pressure that combines with oxygen in air to form sodium oxides, with a melting point of 98°C and boiling point of 883°C. It is a good conductor of electricity and heat, can be easily cut with a knife, and emits a characteristic yellow glow in flame tests due to excited 3s electrons. Sodium metal is highly reactive and reducing, reacting exothermically with water to produce caustic soda and flammable hydrogen gas.

12.name: magnesium
12.description: Magnesium is a chemical element with symbol Mg and atomic number 12. It is a shiny gray metal having a low density, low melting point, and high chemical reactivity. Like the other alkaline earth metals, it occurs naturally only in combination with other elements and almost always has an oxidation state of +2.
12.uses: Magnesium is used primarily as a component in strong and lightweight alloys that contain aluminium. It is essential to all cells and some 300 enzymes in the human body, and magnesium compounds are used medicinally as common laxatives and antacids such as milk of magnesia, and to stabilize abnormal nerve excitation or blood vessel spasm. Magnesium is also widely used as a reducing agent and may be used as an igniter for thermite.
12.characteristics: Magnesium is a gray-white lightweight metal, two-thirds the density of aluminium, with the lowest melting point (650 °C) and lowest boiling point (1,090 °C) of all the alkaline earth metals. Pure polycrystalline magnesium is brittle and easily fractures along shear bands but becomes much more malleable when alloyed with small amounts of other metals. It reacts readily with air to form a thin passivation coating of magnesium oxide that inhibits further corrosion, and the free metal burns with a brilliant-white light.

13.name: aluminium
13.description: Aluminium is a chemical element with symbol Al and atomic number 13. It is a post-transition metal in the boron group that forms compounds primarily in the +3 oxidation state. It has one stable isotope, 27Al, and is the third-most abundant element in Earth's crust after oxygen and silicon.
13.uses: Aluminium is used in transportation, engineering, construction, and packaging. Its high affinity for oxygen makes it suitable as a reducing agent in thermite reactions. It is also used in radiometric dating through the radioactivity of 26Al, and its excellent thermal and electrical conductivity makes it valuable for applications where these properties are needed.
13.characteristics: Aluminium has a density of 2.70 g/cm³, about one-third that of steel, making it much lighter than most common metals. It is soft, ductile, and malleable in pure form, with a silvery white to dull gray appearance and excellent light reflectivity. It is an excellent thermal and electrical conductor, nonmagnetic, and forms a protective oxide layer on its surface when exposed to air.

14.name: silicon
14.description: Silicon is a hard, brittle crystalline solid with a blue-grey metallic lustre. It is a tetravalent non-metal sometimes considered a metalloid and semiconductor, belonging to group 14 of the periodic table. It is relatively unreactive and the eighth most common element in the universe by mass, though it rarely occurs in pure form in the Earth's crust.
14.uses: Silicon is widely used as a semiconductor material in transistors, solar cells, and integrated circuits. It is used commercially in industrial construction with clays, silica sand, and stone, as well as in Portland cement, concrete, ceramics, and glass. Silicon compounds like silicon carbide are used as abrasives and in high-strength ceramics, and silicon is the basis of silicone polymers.
14.characteristics: Silicon has a melting point of 1414 °C and boiling point of 3265 °C, which are the second highest among all metalloids and nonmetals. As a semiconductor, its resistivity decreases as temperature rises due to a small energy gap between its valence and conduction bands. Pure silicon is effectively an insulator at room temperature but becomes conductive when doped with elements such as phosphorus or boron.

15.name: phosphorus
15.description: Phosphorus is a chemical element with symbol P and atomic number 15. All elemental forms of phosphorus are highly reactive and never found in nature, with white phosphorus and red phosphorus being the two most common allotropes. It is a member of the pnictogen family that readily forms a wide variety of organic and inorganic compounds.
15.uses: Phosphorus is essential to all known forms of life through organophosphates including DNA, RNA, ATP, and phospholipids. Industrially, it is primarily used to produce phosphoric acid for phosphate-based fertilizers vital to modern agriculture. Other applications include pesticides, food additives, detergents, and matches, while its flammability can be weaponized in incendiary forms.
15.characteristics: Phosphorus has an occurrence in Earth's crust of about 0.1% and 31P as its only stable isotope. It has main oxidation states of +5, +3 and −3, with a phosphorus atom containing 15 electrons of which 5 are valence electrons. White phosphorus is highly toxic, flammable and pyrophoric with a faint glow when exposed to oxygen, while red phosphorus is less dangerous.

16.name: sulfur
16.description: Sulfur is a chemical element with symbol S and atomic number 16. It is abundant, multivalent and nonmetallic, forming cyclic octatomic molecules with the formula S8 under normal conditions. Elemental sulfur is a bright yellow, crystalline solid at room temperature.
16.uses: The greatest commercial use of sulfur is the production of sulfuric acid for sulfate and phosphate fertilizers and other chemical processes. It is also used in matches, insecticides, and fungicides. Sulfur is an essential element for all life, appearing in amino acids such as cysteine and methionine, vitamins like biotin and thiamine, and cofactors including glutathione and iron-sulfur proteins.
16.characteristics: Octasulfur is a soft, bright-yellow solid that is odorless, melting at 115.21°C and boiling at 444.6°C. It has a density of about 2 g/cm³ and all stable allotropes are excellent electrical insulators. Sulfur is insoluble in water but soluble in carbon disulfide and other nonpolar organic solvents, and it reacts with nearly all other elements except noble gases.

17.name: chlorine
17.description: Chlorine is a chemical element with symbol Cl and atomic number 17, and is the second-lightest of the halogens. It is a yellow-green gas at room temperature that is extremely reactive and a strong oxidising agent, with the highest electron affinity and third-highest electronegativity among the elements. All chlorine in the Earth's crust exists in the form of ionic chloride compounds, and it is the second-most abundant halogen and 20th most abundant element in Earth's crust.
17.uses: Elemental chlorine is commercially produced from brine by electrolysis in the chloralkali process and is used in the manufacture of a wide range of consumer products, including polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and many intermediates for plastics. It is used as a common disinfectant in swimming pools and drinking water, and has served functions in topical antisepsis and public sanitation. The high oxidising potential of elemental chlorine led to the development of commercial bleaches, disinfectants, and chemical reagents for many industrial processes.
17.characteristics: Chlorine is a yellow-green gas at room temperature that melts at −101.0 °C and boils at −34.0 °C, with a melting and boiling point intermediate between fluorine and bromine. It has an electron configuration of [Ne]3s23p5 and is one electron short of a full octet, making it a strong oxidising agent with properties intermediate between fluorine and bromine. The colour fades at low temperatures, so solid chlorine at −195 °C is almost colourless.

18.name: argon
18.description: Argon is a chemical element with symbol Ar and atomic number 18, belonging to group 18 of the periodic table as a noble gas. It is the third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere at 0.934% and the most abundant noble gas in Earth's crust. The name derives from Ancient Greek meaning 'lazy' or 'inactive', referencing its chemical inertness.
18.uses: Argon is used as an inert shielding gas in welding and high-temperature industrial processes such as graphite electric furnaces. It is also used in incandescent and fluorescent lighting, gas-discharge tubes, blue-green gas lasers, and fluorescent glow starters. Additionally, it serves as the target for neutrino experiments and dark matter searches, and is used in the poultry industry for asphyxiation and in fire suppression for valuable equipment.
18.characteristics: Argon is colorless, odorless, nonflammable, and nontoxic in solid, liquid, or gas states. It is chemically inert under most conditions with approximately the same solubility in water as oxygen and is 2.5 times more soluble than nitrogen. Its triple point temperature of 83.8058 K is a defining fixed point in the International Temperature Scale of 1990, and it has low thermal conductivity and desirable electronic properties for certain applications.

19.name: potassium
19.description: Potassium is a chemical element with symbol K and atomic number 19. It is a silvery white metal that is soft enough to easily cut with a knife and is one of the alkali metals with a single valence electron in its outer electron shell. In nature, potassium occurs only in ionic salts, and it is found dissolved in seawater and in many minerals such as orthoclase.
19.uses: Potassium ions are vital for the functioning of all living cells and are necessary for normal nerve transmission. Most industrial applications exploit the high solubility of potassium compounds in water, such as in saltwater soap, and potassium compounds account for 95% of global potassium chemical production through agricultural fertilizers to remediate soil depletion from crop production. Potassium compounds are also used in glass production, bleach, soap, and gunpowder production.
19.characteristics: Potassium metal reacts rapidly with atmospheric oxygen to form flaky white potassium peroxide within seconds, and it reacts vigorously with water generating sufficient heat to ignite hydrogen while burning with a lilac-colored flame. It is unreactive toward nitrogen and saturated hydrocarbons, readily dissolves in liquid ammonia, and has a low first ionization energy of 418.8 kJ/mol making it a strong reducing agent.

20.name: calcium
20.description: Calcium is a chemical element with symbol Ca and atomic number 20, classified as a reactive alkaline earth metal that forms a dark oxide-nitride layer when exposed to air. It is the fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust and the third most abundant metal after iron and aluminium. The name comes from the Latin word calx meaning lime, which was obtained from heating limestone.
20.uses: Calcium compounds are widely used in many industries including foods and pharmaceuticals for calcium supplementation, in the paper industry as bleaches, as components in cement and electrical insulators, and in the manufacture of soaps. The pure metal has few applications due to its high reactivity but is sometimes used in small quantities as an alloying component in steelmaking and in calcium-lead alloys for automotive batteries. Calcium carbide, a major organocalcium compound, is produced in several million tons annually and is used in welding and as a chemical precursor.
20.characteristics: Calcium is a very ductile silvery metal sometimes described as pale yellow, with a melting point of 842°C and boiling point of 1494°C. It has a density of 1.526 g/cm³ at 20°C, the lowest in its group, and is harder than lead but can be cut with a knife with effort. Calcium spontaneously reacts with water to produce calcium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, and forms a mixture of calcium oxide and calcium nitride when exposed to oxygen and nitrogen in air.

21.name: scandium
21.description: Scandium is a silvery-white metallic element with symbol Sc and atomic number 21, found in the d-block of the periodic table and usually classified as a rare-earth element together with yttrium and the lanthanides. It is a soft metal that develops a slightly yellowish or pinkish cast when oxidized by air, and it is susceptible to weathering and dissolves slowly in most dilute acids. In nature, scandium is found exclusively as the stable isotope 45Sc.
21.uses: The main application of scandium is in aluminium-scandium alloys for aerospace industry components, which limit grain growth in welded aluminium and strengthen the material through Al3Sc precipitate formation. Scandium is also used in metal-halide lamps as a high-intensity discharge light source, with approximately 20 kg used annually in the United States for this purpose. Additionally, scandium-stabilized zirconia is used as a high-efficiency electrolyte in solid oxide fuel cells, and scandium is employed as a Lewis acid catalyst in organic chemistry.
21.characteristics: Scandium is a soft metal with intermediate chemical properties between aluminium and yttrium, and it exhibits a diagonal relationship with magnesium similar to the relationship between beryllium and aluminium. The element has low availability as it occurs sparsely in trace amounts in many minerals and is distributed unevenly in Earth's crust at an abundance of 18-25 ppm. Scandium compounds are almost completely dominated by the trivalent ion Sc3+, and while compounds with other oxidation states are rare, they have been well characterized.

22.name: titanium
22.description: Titanium is a chemical element with symbol Ti and atomic number 22. Found in nature only as an oxide, it is a lustrous transition metal with a silver color, low density, and high strength. It is resistant to corrosion in sea water, aqua regia, and chlorine.
22.uses: Titanium alloys are used in aerospace including jet engines, missiles, and spacecraft, as well as military, industrial processes, automotive, agriculture, sporting goods, jewelry, and consumer electronics. Titanium is also highly biocompatible and used in medical applications including prostheses, orthopedic implants, dental implants, and surgical instruments. Titanium dioxide is used as a photocatalyst and in white pigments, while titanium tetrachloride is used in smoke screens and catalysts, and titanium trichloride is used as a catalyst in polypropylene production.
22.characteristics: Titanium is recognized for its high strength-to-weight ratio, being as tensile-strong as some steels but less dense, with a melting point of 1,668 °C. It is paramagnetic with low electrical and thermal conductivity compared to other metals, and forms a protective thin oxide layer upon air exposure that provides excellent corrosion resistance. The metal is ductile, especially in oxygen-free environments, and has the highest tensile-strength-to-density ratio of any metallic element.

23.name: vanadium
23.description: Vanadium is a hard, silvery-grey, malleable transition metal with atomic number 23 and symbol V. The elemental metal is rarely found in nature, but once isolated artificially, an oxide layer forms that somewhat stabilizes it against further oxidation. It is an average-hard, ductile, steel-blue metal that is harder than most metals and steels.
23.uses: Vanadium is mainly used to produce specialty steel alloys such as high-speed tool steels and some aluminium alloys. The most important industrial vanadium compound, vanadium pentoxide, is used as a catalyst for the production of sulfuric acid. The vanadium redox battery for energy storage may be an important application in the future.
23.characteristics: Vanadium is ductile, malleable, and not brittle, with good resistance to corrosion and stability against alkalis and sulfuric and hydrochloric acids. It is oxidized in air at about 933 K (660 °C, 1220 °F), although an oxide passivation layer forms even at room temperature. The chemistry of vanadium is noteworthy for the accessibility of four adjacent oxidation states 2–5, and it forms compounds with a wide variety of colors.

24.name: chromium
24.description: Chromium is a steely-grey, lustrous, hard, and brittle transition metal with atomic number 24 and symbol Cr, representing the first element in group 6 of the periodic table.
24.uses: Chromium is valued for its high corrosion resistance and hardness, with major applications including the production of stainless steel and chrome plating through electroplating, which together comprise 85% of commercial use. It is also greatly valued for its ability to be highly polished while resisting tarnishing, reflecting almost 70% of the visible spectrum and 90% of infrared light.
24.characteristics: Chromium is the third hardest element after carbon and boron with a Mohs hardness of 8.5, has a melting point of 1907 °C and boiling point of 2671 °C, and exhibits unique antiferromagnetic ordering at room temperature. In air, chromium forms a thin protective surface layer of chromium oxide that enhances its corrosion resistance, and it is highly resistant to tarnishing unlike metals such as copper, magnesium, and aluminium.

25.name: manganese
25.description: Manganese is a chemical element with symbol Mn and atomic number 25. It is a hard, brittle, silvery-gray metal often found in minerals in combination with iron, and is a transition metal first isolated in the 1770s.
25.uses: Manganese is used in industrial alloys, particularly in stainless steels where it improves strength, workability, and resistance to wear. Various manganese oxides serve as oxidizing agents, rubber additives, and ingredients in glass making, fertilizers, and ceramics, while manganese sulfate functions as a fungicide. Potassium permanganate is commonly used in laboratories as an oxidizer and in water treatment as a biocide.
25.characteristics: Manganese is a silvery-gray metal that is hard and very brittle, difficult to melt, but oxidizes easily. It tarnishes slowly in air and oxidizes like iron in water containing dissolved oxygen. Manganese and its common ions are paramagnetic, and naturally occurring manganese is composed of one stable isotope, 55Mn.

26.name: iron
26.description: Iron is a chemical element with symbol Fe and atomic number 26. It is a metal belonging to the first transition series and group 8 of the periodic table, and is by mass the most common element on Earth, forming much of Earth's outer and inner core.
26.uses: Iron alloys such as steel, stainless steel, cast iron and special steels are the most common industrial metals due to their mechanical properties and low cost. Iron is also essential to human biology, being a key component of hemoglobin and myoglobin proteins that transport and store oxygen. Additionally, iron is the active site metal in many important redox enzymes involved in cellular respiration and oxidation-reduction processes in plants and animals.
26.characteristics: Pristine pure iron surfaces are mirror-like silvery-gray, but iron readily reacts with oxygen and water to produce brown-to-black hydrated iron oxides known as rust. Below its Curie point of 770°C, iron is ferromagnetic with unpaired electrons that align to create an overall magnetic field. Iron has four stable isotopes and forms compounds in oxidation states ranging from −2 to +7, also forming many coordination complexes with industrial, medical, or research applications.

27.name: cobalt
27.description: Cobalt is a chemical element with symbol Co and atomic number 27. It is found in the Earth's crust only in chemically combined form, except for small deposits in natural meteoric iron alloys. The free element produced by reductive smelting is a hard, lustrous, somewhat brittle, gray metal.
27.uses: Cobalt is primarily used in lithium-ion batteries and in the manufacture of magnetic, wear-resistant and high-strength alloys. Cobalt-based compounds give distinctive blue color to glass, ceramics, inks, paints and varnishes, and cobalt-60 is used as a radioactive tracer and for production of gamma rays. It is also used in the petroleum industry as a catalyst for refining crude oil to remove sulfur, and cobalt is the active center of cobalamins (Vitamin B12), an essential vitamin for all animals.
27.characteristics: Cobalt is a ferromagnetic metal with specific gravity of 8.9 and Curie temperature of 1,115 °C. It is a weakly reducing metal protected from oxidation by a passivating oxide film, and occurs as two crystallographic structures (hcp and fcc) with an ideal transition temperature of 450 °C. Cobalt has common oxidation states of +2 and +3, forms pink [Co(H2O)6]2+ complexes in water, and exists naturally as only one stable isotope, cobalt-59.

28.name: nickel
28.description: Nickel is a chemical element with symbol Ni and atomic number 28. It is a silvery-white lustrous metal with a slight golden tinge that is hard and ductile. Pure nickel is chemically reactive but forms a passivation layer of nickel oxide on its surface that prevents further corrosion.
28.uses: About 68% of world production is used in stainless steel, with a further 10% used for nickel-based and copper-based alloys, 9% for plating, 7% for alloy steels, and 3% in foundries. Nickel is also used in coins, rechargeable batteries including those in electric vehicles, as a catalyst for hydrogenation, cathodes for batteries, pigments, and metal surface treatments.
28.characteristics: Nickel is one of only four elements that are ferromagnetic at or near room temperature, with a Curie temperature of 355°C. It is hard, malleable, and ductile with relatively high electrical and thermal conductivity for transition metals, has a face-centered cubic crystal structure, and can take a high polish.

29.name: copper
29.description: Copper is a chemical element with symbol Cu and atomic number 29. It is a soft, malleable, and ductile metal with very high thermal and electrical conductivity, and a freshly exposed surface of pure copper has a pinkish-orange color.
29.uses: Copper is used as a conductor of heat and electricity, as a building material, and as a constituent of various metal alloys such as sterling silver, cupronickel, and constantan. It is also used in decorative art, as bacteriostatic agents, fungicides, and wood preservatives, and serves essential functions in aerobic organisms particularly in oxygen metabolism.
29.characteristics: Copper has high electrical conductivity of 59.6×106 S/m and the second highest thermal conductivity among pure metals at room temperature. When exposed to air, it slowly oxidizes to form a protective layer of brown-black copper oxide, and can develop a green patina called verdigris on structures. It does not react with water but tarnishes when exposed to sulfur compounds.

30.name: zinc
30.description: Zinc is a chemical element with symbol Zn and atomic number 30. It is a slightly brittle metal at room temperature with a shiny blue whitish appearance when surface oxidation is removed, and is the first element in group 12 of the periodic table. It is the 24th most abundant element in Earth's crust.
30.uses: Zinc has major applications in hot-dip galvanization for plating corrosion-resistant coatings on iron, as well as use in electrical batteries, small non-structural casts, and alloys such as brass. A variety of zinc compounds are used in products including dietary supplements, deodorants, anti-dandruff shampoos, luminescent paints, and in chemical synthesis of organic compounds. Zinc is also an essential trace element for humans, animals, plants, and microorganisms, necessary for prenatal and postnatal development.
30.characteristics: Zinc is a bluish-white, lustrous, diamagnetic metal that is somewhat less dense than iron with a hexagonal crystal structure. It is hard and brittle at most temperatures but becomes malleable between 100 and 150 °C. Zinc has relatively low melting (419.53 °C) and boiling points (907 °C) for a metal, and is a fair conductor of electricity. It has five stable isotopes, with Zn-64 being the most abundant at nearly half of zinc's total abundance.

31.name: gallium
31.description: Gallium is a chemical element with symbol Ga and atomic number 31, discovered by French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran in 1875. It is a soft, silvery metal at standard temperature and pressure with a complex orthorhombic crystal structure, and one of only four non-radioactive metals that is liquid at or near normal room temperature.
31.uses: Gallium is predominantly used in electronics, particularly in the form of gallium arsenide for microwave circuits, high-speed switching circuits, and infrared circuits. Semiconducting gallium nitride and indium gallium nitride produce blue and violet light-emitting diodes and diode lasers, and gallium is also used in the production of artificial gadolinium gallium garnet for jewelry. Additionally, gallium alloys with low melting points are used in thermometers as non-toxic alternatives to mercury, and gallium(III) compounds have been used in some medical applications including pharmaceuticals and radiopharmaceuticals.
31.characteristics: Gallium has a notably low melting point of 29.7646 °C (302.9146 K), just above room temperature, which is used as a temperature reference point on the International Temperature Scale. It exhibits a very large liquid range, with a boiling point of 2,676 K nearly nine times higher than its melting point, and has highly anisotropic physical properties that are strongly temperature-dependent. Unlike mercury, liquid gallium wets most materials and has a low vapor pressure at high temperatures, though its volume expands by 3.10% when changing from liquid to solid.

32.name: germanium
32.description: Germanium is a chemical element with symbol Ge and atomic number 32. It is a lustrous, hard-brittle, grayish-white metalloid in the carbon group that is chemically similar to silicon. Like silicon, germanium naturally reacts and forms complexes with oxygen in nature.
32.uses: Elemental germanium is used as a semiconductor in transistors and various electronic devices, with major end uses including fibre-optic systems, infrared optics, solar cell applications, and light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Germanium compounds are also used for polymerization catalysts and in the production of nanowires, while organogermanium compounds are useful in organometallic chemistry.
32.characteristics: Under standard conditions, germanium is a brittle, silvery-white semiconductor with a metallic luster and diamond cubic crystal structure. It is one of the few substances that expands as it solidifies from the molten state, and has been produced in highly pure crystalline form with impurity of only one part in 10^10. Elemental germanium starts to oxidize slowly in air at around 250 °C, forming germanium dioxide, and occurs mostly in the oxidation state +4 although many +2 compounds are known.

33.name: arsenic
33.description: Arsenic is a chemical element with symbol As and atomic number 33. It is a metalloid and member of group 15, sharing properties with phosphorus and antimony. It occurs naturally in many minerals, usually combined with sulfur and metals, and has various allotropes with the grey form being the most important industrially.
33.uses: The primary use of arsenic is in alloys of lead for car batteries and ammunition. It is used as an n-type dopant in semiconductor electronic devices and as a component of gallium arsenide. Arsenic and its compounds are used in the production of pesticides, treated wood products, herbicides, and insecticides, though these applications are declining due to recognition of arsenic's toxicity.
33.characteristics: Grey arsenic has a double-layered structure with interlocked six-membered rings, is brittle with a Mohs hardness of 3.5, and has a high density of 5.73 g/cm³. Yellow arsenic is soft, waxy, and most toxic with a density of 1.97 g/cm³, while black arsenic is glassy, brittle, and a poor electrical conductor. Arsenic sublimes at 887 K (614 °C) at atmospheric pressure and becomes a semimetal that turns into a semiconductor when amorphized.

34.name: selenium
34.description: Selenium is a chemical element with symbol Se and atomic number 34. It has various physical appearances, including a brick-red powder, a vitreous black solid, and a grey metallic-looking form. It was discovered in 1817 by Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who noted its similarity to tellurium.
34.uses: The chief commercial uses for selenium are glassmaking and pigments. Selenium is a semiconductor used in photocells, and it is still used in some types of DC power surge protectors and fluorescent quantum dots. Selenium is also listed as an ingredient in multivitamins and dietary supplements, and is a component of antioxidant enzymes and deiodinase enzymes.
34.characteristics: Selenium forms several allotropes that interconvert with temperature changes. It can appear as an amorphous brick-red powder, a black vitreous form with polymeric rings, or gray selenium with a hexagonal crystal lattice. Gray selenium is a semiconductor showing appreciable photoconductivity and is insoluble in carbon disulfide, while other forms are insulators and soluble in carbon disulfide.

35.name: bromine
35.description: Bromine is a chemical element with symbol Br and atomic number 35. It is a volatile red-brown liquid at room temperature that evaporates readily to form a similarly colored vapor. Its properties are intermediate between those of chlorine and iodine, and it is one of only two elements that is liquid at standard temperature and pressure.
35.uses: Bromine is used as a fire retardant, with more than half the bromine produced worldwide annually serving this purpose. Bromine compounds are also used in well drilling fluids, photographic film, and as intermediates in the manufacture of organic chemicals, as well as having pharmaceutical applications such as antiepileptics.
35.characteristics: Bromine is a very reactive nonmetal that freezes at −7.2 °C and boils at 58.8 °C. It has a very penetrating, choking, and unpleasant odor derived from the Greek word for stench, and its color results from specific electron transitions between molecular orbitals, appearing pale yellow when solid but reddish-brown as a liquid.

36.name: krypton
36.description: Krypton is a colorless, odorless noble gas with atomic number 36 that occurs in trace amounts in the atmosphere. It is chemically inert and was discovered in Britain in 1898 by William Ramsay and Morris Travers from residue left after evaporating liquid air.
36.uses: Krypton is used in fluorescent lamps, high-powered gas lasers, and photography as a white light source. It is also used in incandescent lamps to reduce filament evaporation, in krypton fluoride lasers for nuclear fusion research, in electromagnetic calorimeters for particle physics, in magnetic resonance imaging, and as an insulating gas between window panes and as a propellant in electric propulsion systems.
36.characteristics: Krypton is characterized by several sharp emission lines with the strongest being green and yellow. Solid krypton is white and has a face-centered cubic crystal structure. It is one of the products of uranium fission and is highly volatile, not staying in solution in near-surface water.

37.name: rubidium
37.description: Rubidium is a chemical element with symbol Rb and atomic number 37. It is a very soft, whitish-grey solid belonging to the alkali metal group, similar to potassium and caesium. Rubidium is the first alkali metal in the group to have a density higher than water.
37.uses: Rubidium metal is easily vaporized and has a convenient spectral absorption range, making it a frequent target for laser manipulation of atoms. Rubidium compounds have various chemical and electronic applications, including use in laser cooling, Bose-Einstein condensation, atomic clocks, and research and development. Rubidium chloride is used to induce living cells to take up DNA and as a biomarker.
37.characteristics: Rubidium is a very soft, ductile, silvery-white metal with a melting point of 39.3 °C and a boiling point of 688 °C. It is the second most electropositive of the stable alkali metals with a very low first ionization energy of only 403 kJ/mol, and due to its strong electropositive nature, it reacts explosively with water. Natural rubidium comprises two isotopes: 72% stable 85Rb and 28% slightly radioactive 87Rb with a half-life of 48.8 billion years.

38.name: strontium
38.description: Strontium is a chemical element with symbol Sr and atomic number 38, and is an alkaline earth metal. It is a soft silver-white yellowish metallic element that is highly chemically reactive and forms a dark oxide layer when exposed to air. It has physical and chemical properties similar to calcium and barium, occurring naturally mainly in the minerals celestine and strontianite.
38.uses: During the 19th century, strontium was mostly used in the production of sugar from sugar beets. At the peak of television cathode-ray tube production, as much as 75% of strontium consumption in the United States was used for the faceplate glass. Volatile strontium salts are used in pyrotechnics and in the production of flares, and the isotope 89Sr is used to treat bone cancer.
38.characteristics: Strontium is a divalent silvery metal with a pale yellow tint, softer than calcium and harder than barium. Its melting point is 777 °C and boiling point is 1377 °C, with a density of 2.64 g/cm³. It is intermediate in reactivity between calcium and barium, and finely powdered strontium metal is pyrophoric, meaning it will ignite spontaneously in air at room temperature.

39.name: yttrium
39.description: Yttrium is a silvery-metallic transition metal with symbol Y and atomic number 39 that is chemically similar to the lanthanides and is often classified as a rare-earth element. It is a soft, lustrous and highly crystalline metal that is almost always found in combination with lanthanide elements in rare-earth minerals and is never found in nature as a free element. The pure element is relatively stable in air in bulk form due to a protective oxide film, but when finely divided, it is very unstable and can ignite at temperatures exceeding 400 °C.
39.uses: The most important present-day use of yttrium is as a component of phosphors, especially those used in LEDs, and historically it was widely used in red phosphors in television cathode ray tube displays. Yttrium is also used in the production of electrodes, electrolytes, electronic filters, lasers, superconductors, various medical applications, and for tracing materials to enhance their properties.
39.characteristics: Yttrium is a soft, silvery-metallic, lustrous and highly crystalline metal in group 3 that is less electronegative than scandium but has significantly stronger similarities to the lanthanides than to its periodic table neighbors. The pure element forms a protective Y2O3 oxide film on its surface that can reach 10 μm thickness when heated to 750 °C in water vapor, and it exists almost exclusively in the +3 oxidation state forming various inorganic compounds. Yttrium's Y3+ ion is colorless in solution due to the absence of electrons in the d and f electron shells.

40.name: zirconium
40.description: Zirconium is a chemical element with symbol Zr and atomic number 40. It is a lustrous transition metal with a greyish-white color that is solid at room temperature, ductile, malleable, and corrosion-resistant.
40.uses: Zirconium and its alloys are mainly used as a refractory and opacifier. Zirconium alloys are used to clad nuclear fuel rods due to their low neutron absorption and corrosion resistance, in space vehicles and turbine blades for high heat resistance, in flashbulbs, dental implants and prosthetics, deodorant, and water purification systems.
40.characteristics: Zirconium is a soft metal that is highly resistant to corrosion by alkalis, acids, and salt water, though it dissolves in hydrochloric and sulfuric acid in the presence of fluorine. It has a melting point of 1855°C and a boiling point of 4409°C. In powder form it is highly flammable, but the solid form is much less prone to ignition.

41.name: niobium
41.description: Niobium is a light grey, crystalline transition metal with symbol Nb and atomic number 41. It is a lustrous, ductile, paramagnetic metal that is slightly less electropositive and more compact than zirconium, with chemical properties very similar to tantalum.
41.uses: Niobium is used mostly in alloys, particularly in special steels such as those used in gas pipelines, where it enhances strength by scavenging carbide and nitride. It is used in superconducting materials for MRI scanner magnets, jet and rocket engines, welding, nuclear industries, electronics, optics, and jewelry. The metal is also used in nuclear industries where neutron-transparent structures are desired due to its low neutron capture cross-section.
41.characteristics: Pure niobium has a Mohs hardness rating similar to pure titanium and ductility similar to iron. It oxidizes very slowly in Earth's atmosphere and is corrosion-resistant. Niobium becomes a superconductor at cryogenic temperatures with the highest critical temperature of elemental superconductors at 9.2 K, and it has the greatest magnetic penetration depth of any element. When very pure, it is comparatively soft and ductile, but impurities make it harder.

42.name: molybdenum
42.description: Molybdenum is a chemical element with symbol Mo and atomic number 42. It is a silvery-grey metal that does not occur naturally as a free metal on Earth but is found only in oxidized states in minerals. The element was discovered in 1778 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele and first isolated as a metal in 1781 by Peter Jacob Hjelm.
42.uses: About 80% of world molybdenum production is used in steel alloys, including high-strength alloys and superalloys, because it readily forms hard, stable carbides. Approximately 14% of world production is used in molybdenum compounds serving as pigments and catalysts. Molybdenum is also essential for biological processes, particularly in nitrogen fixation enzymes in bacteria and cyanobacteria, and is essential for all higher eukaryotic organisms including humans.
42.characteristics: Molybdenum is a silvery-grey metal with a Mohs hardness of 5.5 and has the sixth-highest melting point of any element at 2,623 °C. It has one of the lowest coefficients of thermal expansion among commercially used metals and does not visibly react with oxygen or water at room temperature. Most molybdenum compounds have low solubility in water, and the element is a transition metal with an electronegativity of 2.16 on the Pauling scale.

43.name: technetium
43.description: Technetium is a chemical element with symbol Tc and atomic number 43. It is the lightest element whose isotopes are all radioactive, and it is one of only two radioactive elements both preceded and succeeded in the periodic table by elements with stable forms. It is a silvery gray, crystalline transition metal that lies between manganese and rhenium in group 7 of the periodic table.
43.uses: Technetium-99m, a short-lived gamma-ray-emitting nuclear isomer, is used in nuclear medicine for a wide variety of tests such as bone cancer diagnoses, with approximately ten million medical diagnostic procedures annually. The ground state of technetium-99 is used as a gamma-ray-free source of beta particles. Long-lived technetium isotopes produced commercially are byproducts of uranium-235 fission in nuclear reactors and are extracted from nuclear fuel rods.
43.characteristics: Technetium is a silvery-gray radioactive metal with an appearance similar to platinum, commonly obtained as a gray powder with a hexagonal close-packed crystal structure. It exhibits nine oxidation states from −1 to +7, with +4, +5, and +7 being most common, and its chemical properties are intermediate between those of manganese and rhenium. Pure metallic single-crystal technetium becomes a type-II superconductor at temperatures below 7.46 K, and it slowly tarnishes in moist air and burns in powder form when exposed to oxygen.

44.name: ruthenium
44.description: Ruthenium is a rare transition metal belonging to the platinum group of the periodic table with symbol Ru and atomic number 44. It is a polyvalent hard white metal that is unreactive to most chemicals. The element was discovered in 1844 by Karl Ernst Claus at Kazan State University and named in honor of Russia.
44.uses: Most ruthenium produced is used in wear-resistant electrical contacts and thick-film resistors. It is also used in platinum alloys, as a chemical catalyst, and as a capping layer for extreme ultraviolet photomasks in semiconductor lithography. Ruthenium tetroxide is used as an intermediate in the purification of ruthenium from ores and radiowastes.
44.characteristics: Ruthenium is a hard white metal that does not tarnish at ambient conditions but oxidizes upon heating to 800°C. It has four crystal modifications and is not attacked by acids including aqua regia, but is attacked by sodium hypochlorite at room temperature and halogens at high temperatures. Small amounts of ruthenium increase the hardness of platinum and palladium, and it can increase the corrosion resistance of titanium markedly.

45.name: rhodium
45.description: Rhodium is a rare, dark silvery-white, hard, corrosion-resistant transition metal with symbol Rh and atomic number 45. It is a noble metal and member of the platinum group, with only one naturally occurring isotope. It is one of the rarest and most valuable precious metals.
45.uses: Rhodium is primarily used as a catalyst in three-way catalytic converters in automobiles, consuming about 80% of world production. It is also used for enhancement of jewelry, electroplating on white gold and platinum, rhodium-plating of sterling silver to resist tarnishing, in catalytic processes for acetic acid production, asymmetric hydrogenation for drug precursors, and in neutron detectors for nuclear reactors.
45.characteristics: Rhodium is a hard, silvery, durable metal with high reflectance that does not normally form an oxide even when heated. It has both a higher melting point and lower density than platinum, and is not attacked by most acids, being completely insoluble in nitric acid and dissolving only slightly in aqua regia.

46.name: palladium
46.description: Palladium is a rare and lustrous silvery-white metal with chemical symbol Pd and atomic number 46. It was discovered in 1802 by English chemist William Hyde Wollaston and belongs to the platinum group metals. It is the least dense and has the lowest melting point of the platinum group metals.
46.uses: More than half the supply of palladium is used in catalytic converters, which convert harmful gases in automobile exhaust into nontoxic substances. Palladium is also used in electronics, dentistry, medicine, hydrogen purification, chemical applications, jewelry, and as catalysts in organic chemistry reactions.
46.characteristics: Palladium is a soft silver-white metal that is soft and ductile when annealed, becoming harder when cold-worked. It does not react with oxygen at standard temperature and thus does not tarnish in air. It dissolves slowly in concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids, readily in aqua regia at room temperature, and dissolves readily in aqua regia.

47.name: silver
47.description: A soft, white, lustrous transition metal with symbol Ag and atomic number 47. It exhibits the highest electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity and reflectivity of any metal, and is found in the Earth's crust in pure form, as alloys, and in various minerals.
47.uses: Silver is used in photovoltaics, electrical contacts and conductors, printed electronics, brazing alloys, catalysis, specialized mirrors and window coatings, and antimicrobial materials. Silver halides are important in photographic film, photographic paper and photochromic glass. Historically it has been valued as a precious metal and coinage metal with an enduring role in monetary systems, jewellery, tableware and decorative arts.
47.characteristics: Silver is a relatively soft, extremely ductile and malleable metal with a brilliant white metallic lustre that can take a high polish. It has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of all metals and the lowest contact resistance of any metal. Silver is a rather unreactive metal and does not react with air even at red heat, though it readily tarnishes when exposed to sulfur and its compounds.

48.name: cadmium
48.description: Cadmium is a soft, silvery-white metal with symbol Cd and atomic number 48. It is chemically similar to zinc and mercury in group 12, demonstrating an oxidation state of +2 in most compounds. The average concentration of cadmium in Earth's crust is between 0.1 and 0.5 parts per million.
48.uses: Cadmium was historically used as a corrosion-resistant plating on steel, and cadmium compounds serve as red, orange, and yellow pigments, colorants for glass, and plastic stabilizers. It is used as a neutron poison in nuclear reactor control rods, in nickel-cadmium batteries, and in cadmium telluride solar panels, though many applications have declined due to toxicity concerns.
48.characteristics: Cadmium is a soft, malleable, ductile, silvery-white metal that is resistant to corrosion and insoluble in water in bulk form. It burns in air to form brown amorphous cadmium oxide and is not flammable in bulk, though its powdered form may burn and release toxic fumes. Naturally occurring cadmium is composed of eight isotopes, two of which are radioactive.

49.name: indium
49.description: Indium is a silvery-white post-transition metal and one of the softest elements with atomic number 49. It is highly ductile with a bright luster and so soft that it can be cut with a knife. Chemically, its properties are largely intermediate between gallium and thallium.
49.uses: Indium is used primarily in the production of flat-panel displays as indium tin oxide (ITO), a transparent and conductive coating. It is also used in the semiconductor industry in low-melting-point metal alloys such as solders and soft-metal high-vacuum seals, and in the manufacture of blue and white LED circuits.
49.characteristics: Indium has a Mohs hardness of 1.2, a melting point of 156.60 °C, and a boiling point of 2072 °C. It has a density of 7.31 g/cm³, becomes a superconductor below 3.41 K, and displays greater solubility in liquid mercury than any other metal. When bent, it produces a high-pitched crackling sound due to crystal twinning.

50.name: tin
50.description: Tin is a chemical element with symbol Sn and atomic number 50. It is a soft, metallic-gray post-transition metal in group 14 of the periodic table that is soft enough to be cut with little force and can be bent by hand with little effort.
50.uses: Tin is used in many alloys including bronze, pewter, and tin-lead soft solders. It is used in the manufacture of transparent, electrically conducting films of indium tin oxide in optoelectronic applications, and is widely used for corrosion-resistant tin plating of steel, particularly for food packaging in tin cans. Tin-plated steel is preferred because of the low toxicity of inorganic tin.
50.characteristics: Tin is soft, malleable, ductile, and highly crystalline with a silvery-white color. When bent, a bar of tin produces a crackling sound called the tin cry from the twinning of crystals. It melts at about 232°C and boils at 2,602°C. Tin has two main allotropes: β-tin (white tin), which is stable at room temperature and malleable, and α-tin (gray tin), which is stable below 13.2°C and brittle with a diamond cubic structure. Metallic tin does not easily oxidize in air or water.

51.name: antimony
51.description: Antimony is a chemical element with the symbol Sb and atomic number 51. It is a lustrous grey metal or metalloid that occurs in nature mainly as the sulfide mineral stibnite (Sb2S3). A silvery, lustrous gray solid that is stable in air at room temperature, it is a member of group 15 of the periodic table.
51.uses: Antimony compounds have been known since ancient history and were powdered for use as cosmetics (kohl) and medicine. The most common applications for metallic antimony are in alloys with lead and tin for solders, bullets, and plain bearings, and it improves the rigidity of lead-alloy plates in lead-acid batteries. Antimony trioxide is used as an additive for halogen-containing flame retardants, and antimony is used as a dopant in semiconductor devices.
51.characteristics: Antimony has an electronegativity of 2.05 and a Mohs scale hardness of 3. It is a silvery, lustrous gray solid with a high density of 6.697 g/cm³, but exhibits low hardness and brittleness due to weak bonding between its layers. When heated, it reacts with oxygen to produce antimony trioxide, and it is attacked by oxidizing acids.

52.name: tellurium
52.description: Tellurium is a chemical element with symbol Te and atomic number 52. It is a brittle, mildly toxic, rare, silver-white metalloid that is chemically related to selenium and sulfur as a member of the chalcogens. It is far more common in the universe than on Earth due to the loss of its volatile hydride during Earth's formation.
52.uses: The primary commercial use of tellurium is in CdTe solar panels and thermoelectric devices. It is also used in copper and steel alloys where it improves machinability, and historically was investigated as an engine knock preventative in fuel.
52.characteristics: Tellurium has two allotropes: crystalline tellurium that is silvery-white with metallic luster and brittle, and amorphous tellurium that is a black-brown powder. It is a semiconductor with greater electrical conductivity in certain directions and increased conductivity when exposed to light, with the highest melting and boiling points among the chalcogens at 722.66 and 1,261 K respectively.

53.name: iodine
53.description: Iodine is a chemical element with symbol I and atomic number 53. It is the heaviest of the stable halogens and exists at standard conditions as a semi-lustrous, non-metallic solid that melts to form a deep violet liquid at 114 °C and boils to a violet gas at 184 °C. The element was discovered by French chemist Bernard Courtois in 1811 and named by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac after the Ancient Greek word for 'violet'.
53.uses: As the heaviest essential mineral nutrient, iodine is required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones and is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. Due to its high atomic number and ease of attachment to organic compounds, iodine is used as a non-toxic radiocontrast material, and radioactive isotopes of iodine can be used to treat thyroid cancer. It is also used as a catalyst in the industrial production of acetic acid and some polymers.
53.characteristics: Iodine is the weakest oxidizing agent among the stable halogens with an electronegativity of 2.66 on the Pauling scale and has the lowest first ionization energy and lowest reactivity among stable halogens. It is slightly soluble in water and forms diatomic molecules with the chemical formula I₂, appearing violet as a solid and gas but brown in polar solutions due to charge-transfer complexes. Iodine has the largest atomic radius among stable halogens and is a two-dimensional semiconductor with the weakest interhalogen bond among stable halogens.

54.name: xenon
54.description: Xenon is a chemical element with symbol Xe and atomic number 54. It is a dense, colorless, odorless noble gas found in Earth's atmosphere in trace amounts. Although generally unreactive, it can undergo chemical reactions such as the formation of xenon hexafluoroplatinate, the first noble gas compound to be synthesized.
54.uses: Xenon is used in flash lamps and arc lamps, and as a general anesthetic. It is used in excimer laser designs and as a pump in laser designs. Xenon is also used to search for hypothetical weakly interacting massive particles and as a propellant for ion thrusters in spacecraft.
54.characteristics: Xenon has a density of 5.894 kg/m³ at standard temperature and pressure, about 4.5 times the density of Earth's atmosphere. As a liquid, it has high polarizability and is an excellent solvent capable of dissolving hydrocarbons, biological molecules, and water. Under gigapascals of pressure, xenon forms a metallic phase that appears sky blue, and when excited by electrical discharge in a gas-filled tube, it emits a blue or lavenderish glow.

55.name: caesium
55.description: Caesium is a soft, silvery-golden alkali metal with symbol Cs and atomic number 55. It has a melting point of 28.5°C, making it one of only five elemental metals that are liquid at or near room temperature. It is the least electronegative stable element and has the largest atomic radius of all elements whose radii have been measured or calculated.
55.uses: Caesium is widely used in highly accurate atomic clocks and has been used to define the basic unit of time, the second, since 1967. Since the 1990s, the largest application has been as caesium formate for drilling fluids, with additional uses in electricity production, electronics, and chemistry. The radioactive isotope caesium-137 is used in medical applications, industrial gauges, and hydrology.
55.characteristics: Caesium is pyrophoric and reacts with water explosively even at temperatures as low as −116°C. It is highly ductile and the softest of all solid elements at room temperature with a Mohs hardness of 0.2. Its golden colour results from the decreasing frequency of light required to excite electrons, and it has a low boiling point of 641°C, the lowest of all stable metals other than mercury.

56.name: barium
56.description: Barium is a chemical element with symbol Ba and atomic number 56, belonging to group 2 as the fifth element. It is a soft, silvery alkaline earth metal that is highly chemically reactive and never found in nature as a free element.
56.uses: Barium has been used as a getter in vacuum tubes, as an emissive coating on cathodes, and is a component of high-temperature superconductors and electroceramics. Barium compounds are added to fireworks for green color, barium sulfate is used in oil well drilling fluids and as an X-ray radiocontrast agent for imaging the gastrointestinal tract, and water-soluble barium compounds have been used as rodenticides.
56.characteristics: Barium is a soft, silvery-white metal with high electrical conductivity that rapidly oxidizes in air to form a dark gray layer. It has a Mohs hardness of 1.25, a melting point of 1,000 K, and a density of 3.62 g/cm³, adopting a body-centered cubic structure at room temperature.

57.name: lanthanum
57.description: Lanthanum is a soft, ductile, silvery-white metal with symbol La and atomic number 57. It is the first element and prototype of the lanthanide series, a group of 15 similar elements in the periodic table, and is traditionally counted among the rare-earth elements. Its usual oxidation state is +3, although some compounds with an oxidation state of +2 are known.
57.uses: Lanthanum compounds have numerous applications including catalysts, additives in glass, carbon arc lamps for studio lights and projectors, ignition elements in lighters and torches, electron cathodes, scintillators, and gas tungsten arc welding electrodes. Lanthanum carbonate is used as a phosphate binder to treat high levels of phosphate in the blood accompanied by kidney failure.
57.characteristics: Lanthanum is a soft metal that tarnishes slowly when exposed to air and can readily burn to form lanthanum(III) oxide. It has a relatively high electrical resistivity of 615 nΩm at room temperature, a hexagonal crystal structure at room temperature, and a melting point of 920 °C. Among the lanthanides, lanthanum is exceptional in having no 4f electrons as a single gas-phase atom and is the least volatile of the lanthanides.

58.name: cerium
58.description: Cerium is a soft, ductile, and silvery-white metal that is the second element in the lanthanide series with atomic number 58. It tarnishes when exposed to air and is considered one of the rare-earth elements. Cerium often shows an oxidation state of +3 characteristic of the lanthanide series, but also has a stable +4 state that does not oxidize water.
58.uses: Cerium(IV) oxide is used to polish glass and is an important part of catalytic converters. Cerium metal is used in ferrocerium lighters for its pyrophoric properties. Cerium-doped YAG phosphor is used in conjunction with blue light-emitting diodes to produce white light in most commercial white LED light sources.
58.characteristics: Cerium is a ductile metal with a hardness similar to that of silver, and its estimated abundance in the Earth's crust is 68 ppm. It is highly electropositive and reacts with water, and metallic cerium can be highly pyrophoric. Cerium has a variable electronic structure and exhibits four allotropic forms at standard pressure with different crystal structures depending on temperature.

59.name: praseodymium
59.description: Praseodymium is a chemical element with symbol Pr and atomic number 59, the third member of the lanthanide series and a rare-earth metal. It is a soft, silvery, malleable and ductile metal that is too reactive to be found in native form, developing a green oxide coating when exposed to air.
59.uses: Praseodymium is valued for its magnetic, electrical, chemical, and optical properties, with many industrial uses involving its ability to filter yellow light from light sources.
59.characteristics: It is a ductile metal with hardness comparable to silver, paramagnetic at all temperatures above 1 K, and forms a double hexagonal close-packed crystal structure at room temperature. Praseodymium most readily forms the +3 oxidation state and produces yellowish-green aqueous ions and various shades of yellow-green when incorporated into glasses.

60.name: neodymium
60.description: Neodymium is a chemical element with symbol Nd and atomic number 60, the fourth member of the lanthanide series and one of the rare-earth metals. It is a hard, slightly malleable, silvery metal that quickly tarnishes in air and moisture. When oxidized, neodymium reacts quickly, producing pink, purple/blue, and yellow compounds in various oxidation states.
60.uses: Neodymium compounds are used as glass dyes and additives, with glasses doped with neodymium used in lasers emitting infrared wavelengths. Neodymium alloys are used to make high-strength permanent magnets widely used in microphones, loudspeakers, headphones, electric motors, and computer hard disk drives. Larger neodymium magnets are used in electric motors with high power-to-weight ratios in hybrid cars and in generators for aircraft and wind turbines.
60.characteristics: Metallic neodymium has a bright, silvery metallic luster and exists in two allotropic forms with a transformation at about 863°C. It is paramagnetic at room temperature but becomes an antiferromagnet below 20 K, exhibiting complex magnetic phases. Neodymium has a melting point of 1,024°C and boiling point of 3,074°C, usually has oxidation state +3 but can form +2 and +4 states, and corrodes completely in about a year when exposed to ambient conditions.

61.name: promethium
61.description: Promethium is a chemical element with symbol Pm and atomic number 61. All of its isotopes are radioactive, and it is extremely rare with only about 500–600 grams naturally occurring in the Earth's crust at any given time. Chemically, promethium is a lanthanide that shows only one stable oxidation state of +3.
61.uses: Promethium-147 is the only isotope with practical applications, with chemical compounds used in luminous paint, atomic batteries, and thickness-measurement devices. Because natural promethium is exceedingly scarce, it is typically synthesized by bombarding uranium-235 with thermal neutrons to produce promethium-147 as a fission product.
61.characteristics: Promethium has a double hexagonal close packed (dhcp) structure and a hardness of 63 kg/mm² at low temperature, converting to a body-centered cubic (bcc) phase upon heating to 890 °C. Its melting point, ionization energies, and other properties are intermediate between those of neodymium and samarium, and it has an atomic radius that is the second largest among all lanthanides. Compounds of promethium tend to be pink or red in color.

62.name: samarium
62.description: Samarium is a moderately hard silvery metal with symbol Sm and atomic number 62 that slowly oxidizes in air. As a typical lanthanide series member, it usually has an oxidation state of +3, though samarium(II) compounds are also known.
62.uses: The main commercial use is in samarium-cobalt magnets for permanent magnetization. Samarium-153 is used in the drug lexidronam to treat cancer, while samarium-149 is added to nuclear reactor control rods as a neutron absorber. Other applications include catalysis, radioactive dating, X-ray lasers, and samarium(II) iodide as a reducing agent in chemical synthesis.
62.characteristics: Samarium has hardness and density similar to zinc with a boiling point of 1,794 °C, making it the third most volatile lanthanide. It has one of the largest atomic radii among elements at 238 pm and exhibits paramagnetism at room temperature. The metal slowly oxidizes in air at room temperature and spontaneously ignites at 150 °C.

63.name: europium
63.description: Europium is a silvery-white metal of the lanthanide series with atomic number 63 and symbol Eu. It is the most chemically reactive, least dense, and softest of the lanthanides, soft enough to be cut with a knife. It reacts readily with air to form a dark oxide coating and was discovered in 1896, then named after the continent of Europe in 1901.
63.uses: Most applications of europium exploit the phosphorescence of europium compounds. Divalent europium in small amounts is the activator of the bright blue fluorescence of some samples of the mineral fluorite. In astrophysics, the signature of europium in stellar spectra can be used to classify stars and inform theories of stellar formation.
63.characteristics: Europium is a ductile metal with hardness similar to that of lead that crystallizes in a body-centered cubic lattice. It rapidly oxidizes in air and has reactivity with water comparable to that of calcium, igniting at 150 to 180 °C. Although usually trivalent, europium readily forms divalent compounds with an electron configuration of 4f7, which is unusual among lanthanides.

64.name: gadolinium
64.description: Gadolinium is a silvery-white, malleable and ductile rare-earth element with atomic number 64. It is the eighth member of the lanthanide series and crystallizes in a hexagonal close-packed structure at room temperature. Below 20°C it is ferromagnetic, and above this temperature it is the most paramagnetic element.
64.uses: Gadolinium is used as a contrast agent for MRI scans, in nuclear reactors as a neutron absorber and burnable poison, in alloys to improve workability and resistance to oxidation at high temperatures, as a phosphor in medical imaging, as a gamma ray emitter, in electronic and optical devices, and in superconductors. It is also used in neutron radiography and neutron capture therapy.
64.characteristics: Gadolinium reacts slowly with atmospheric oxygen or moisture to form a black oxide coating, and tarnishes quickly in moist air. It is a strong reducing agent and quite electropositive, reacting slowly with cold water and quickly with hot water. The isotope gadolinium-157 has the highest thermal-neutron capture cross-section among any stable nuclide at about 259,000 barns, and gadolinium demonstrates a magnetocaloric effect where its temperature increases when entering a magnetic field and decreases when leaving one.

65.name: terbium
65.description: Terbium is a silvery-white rare earth metal and the ninth member of the lanthanide series with atomic number 65. It is malleable, ductile, and fairly electropositive, reacting with water to evolve hydrogen gas. Terbium is never found in nature as a free element but is contained in many minerals including cerite, gadolinite, monazite, xenotime and euxenite.
65.uses: Terbium is used to dope calcium fluoride, calcium tungstate and strontium molybdate in solid-state devices, and as a crystal stabilizer of fuel cells that operate at elevated temperatures. As a component of Terfenol-D, terbium is used in actuators, naval sonar systems and sensors. Most of the world's terbium supply is used in green phosphors, with terbium oxide used in fluorescent lamps and television and monitor cathode-ray tubes, and terbium green phosphors combined with europium phosphors to provide trichromatic white lighting technology.
65.characteristics: Terbium is silvery-white, malleable, ductile and soft enough to be cut with a knife, with relatively high stability in air compared to more reactive lanthanides. The terbium(III) cation is brilliantly fluorescent in a bright lemon-yellow color, and it has a simple ferromagnetic ordering below 219 K that transforms into a helical antiferromagnetic state above that temperature. Terbium readily oxidizes in the presence of most acids, halogens, and water.

66.name: dysprosium
66.description: Dysprosium is a chemical element with symbol Dy and atomic number 66. It is a rare-earth element in the lanthanide series with a metallic silver luster. It is never found in nature as a free element but is found in various minerals such as xenotime.
