66.uses: Dysprosium is used to produce neodymium-iron-boron magnets crucial for electric vehicle motors and wind turbines. It is used for its high thermal neutron absorption cross-section in control rods in nuclear reactors, for its high magnetic susceptibility in data-storage applications, and as a component of Terfenol-D, a magnetostrictive material. It is also used in laser materials, commercial lighting, infrared radiation sources, dosimeters, and nanofibers for reinforcement and catalysis.
66.characteristics: Dysprosium has a bright metallic silver luster and is soft, capable of being machined without sparking if overheating is avoided. It has the highest magnetic strength of the elements, especially at low temperatures, with a Curie temperature of 90.5 K. Its physical characteristics can be greatly affected by even small amounts of impurities, and soluble dysprosium salts are mildly toxic while insoluble salts are considered non-toxic.

67.name: holmium
67.description: Holmium is a rare-earth element and the eleventh member of the lanthanide series with atomic number 67. It is a relatively soft, silvery, fairly corrosion-resistant and malleable metal that is too reactive to be found in native form, slowly forming a yellowish oxide coating when exposed to air.
67.uses: Holmium is used to create the strongest artificially generated magnetic fields when placed within high-strength magnets as a magnetic pole piece. Its compounds are used in certain laser and glass-colorant applications, and it is used as a burnable poison in nuclear reactors due to its strong absorption of neutrons. Glass containing holmium oxide is used as a calibration standard for optical spectrophotometers, and holmium-doped yttrium iron garnet has applications in solid-state lasers and optical isolators.
67.characteristics: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment (10.6 μB) of any naturally occurring element and the highest magnetic permeability and magnetic saturation of any element. It has a boiling point of 3,000 K and is ferromagnetic below 19 K, and its trivalent ions have fluorescent properties with unique emission light lines that appear yellowish or orange-red depending on lighting conditions.

68.name: erbium
68.description: Erbium is a chemical element with symbol Er and atomic number 68. It is a silvery-white solid metal when artificially isolated and a lanthanide, rare-earth element originally found in the gadolinite mine in Ytterby, Sweden. Natural erbium is always found in chemical combination with other elements.
68.uses: Erbium's principal uses involve its pink-colored Er3+ ions for optical fluorescent properties in laser applications, particularly in erbium-doped fiber amplifiers for optical communications at 1550 nm wavelength. Medical applications in dermatology and dentistry rely on erbium ion's 2940 nm emission for laser surgery and dental procedures. Erbium compounds are also used as phosphor activators, in infrared-absorbing glass, and in crystal growth applications.
68.characteristics: Pure erbium metal is malleable, soft, and stable in air without rapid oxidation. Its salts are rose-colored, and the element exhibits characteristic sharp absorption spectra bands in visible light, ultraviolet, and near infrared. Erbium is ferromagnetic below 19 K, antiferromagnetic between 19 and 80 K, and paramagnetic above 80 K, and it burns readily in oxygen to form erbium(III) oxide while reacting slowly with cold water and quickly with hot water.

69.name: thulium
69.description: Thulium is a chemical element with symbol Tm and atomic number 69, the thirteenth element in the lanthanide series of metals. It is the second-least abundant lanthanide in the Earth's crust, after radioactively unstable promethium. It is an easily workable metal with a bright silvery-gray luster that is fairly soft and slowly tarnishes in air.
69.uses: Thulium is used as a dopant in solid-state lasers, particularly in holmium-chromium-thulium triple-doped yttrium aluminium garnet (Ho:Cr:Tm:YAG) lasers for military, medical, and meteorology applications. Artificial radioactive isotopes of thulium, especially thulium-170, are used as radiation sources in portable X-ray devices for medical and dental diagnosis and industrial radiography. Thulium has also been used in high-temperature superconductors, ferrites for microwave equipment, arc lighting, euro banknotes as a counterfeiting measure, and as a luminescent material in dosimeters and proposed solar concentrator windows.
69.characteristics: Pure thulium metal has a bright silvery luster with a Mohs hardness of 2 to 3, making it malleable and ductile. It is ferromagnetic below 32 K, antiferromagnetic between 32 and 56 K, and paramagnetic above 56 K, with two major allotropes: tetragonal α-Tm and hexagonal β-Tm. The metal tarnishes slowly in air, burns readily at 150 °C to form thulium(III) oxide, reacts slowly with cold water and quickly with hot water, and its most common oxidation state is +3, with Tm³⁺ ions in solution exhibiting bright blue luminescence and existing as nine-coordinate water complexes.

70.name: ytterbium
70.description: Ytterbium is a chemical element with symbol Yb and atomic number 70. It is a soft, malleable and ductile metal that is the fourteenth element in the lanthanide series, distinguished by the relative stability of its +2 oxidation state and its closed-shell electron configuration.
70.uses: Ytterbium is mainly used as a dopant of stainless steel or active laser media, and less often as a gamma ray source. Microscopic traces are used as a dopant in the Yb:YAG laser, and some ytterbium halides are used as reagents in organic synthesis, tooth fillings, and X-ray contrast agents.
70.characteristics: Ytterbium is a rare-earth element with notably lower density, melting point, and boiling point than most other lanthanides due to its closed-shell electron configuration. It has a melting point of 824°C and boiling point of 1196°C, is readily dissolved by strong mineral acids, tarnishes slowly in air taking on a golden or brown hue, and forms both divalent and trivalent compounds, with the divalent state being unusual for lanthanides.

71.name: lutetium
71.description: Lutetium is a silvery white metal with atomic number 71, classified as the last element in the lanthanide series and also as the first element of the sixth-period transition metals. It resists corrosion in dry air but not in moist air. Lutetium is the smallest lanthanide atom due to lanthanide contraction, and it has the highest density, melting point, and hardness among the lanthanides.
71.uses: Lutetium-176 is used to determine the age of minerals and meteorites. 177Lu-DOTA-TATE is used for radionuclide therapy on neuroendocrine tumours. Stable lutetium can be used as catalysts in petroleum cracking and in alkylation, hydrogenation, and polymerization applications. Lutetium compounds are used in high refractive index immersion lithography and as dopants in gadolinium gallium garnet for magnetic bubble memory devices, as well as in positron emission tomography detectors.
71.characteristics: Lutetium is a silvery white metal that burns readily at 150°C to form lutetium oxide. It has the highest Brinell hardness of any lanthanide at 890–1300 MPa and the highest density and melting point among lanthanides. Lutetium generally exists in the +3 oxidation state and its compounds form colorless aqueous solutions that typically produce white crystalline solids, except for the brown iodide.

72.name: hafnium
72.description: Hafnium is a lustrous, silvery gray, tetravalent transition metal with atomic number 72 and symbol Hf. It chemically resembles zirconium and is found in many zirconium minerals. The element is ductile and corrosion-resistant, forming a protective oxide film in air.
72.uses: Hafnium is most often used in alloys with nickel and was historically used in larger quantities to produce control rods for nuclear reactors due to its large neutron capture cross section. It is used in filaments and electrodes, and semiconductor fabrication processes use its oxide for integrated circuits at 45 nanometres and smaller, while superalloys can contain hafnium in combination with niobium, titanium, or tungsten.
72.characteristics: Hafnium is a shiny, silvery, ductile metal that is corrosion-resistant, changing from a hexagonal close-packed lattice to a body-centered cubic lattice at 2,388 K. Pure hafnium is extremely flammable and pyrophoric, capable of spontaneous combustion in air, and despite forming a protective oxide film, it is attacked by hydrofluoric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid. It has a notably higher density than zirconium and a high thermal neutron capture cross section roughly three orders of magnitude greater than that of zirconium.

73.name: tantalum
73.description: Tantalum is a chemical element with symbol Ta and atomic number 73, named after Tantalus in Greek mythology. It is a very hard, ductile, lustrous, blue-gray transition metal that is highly corrosion-resistant and belongs to the refractory metals group. It is a group 5 element occurring geologically with niobium, mainly in mineral groups tantalite and columbite.
73.uses: Tantalum is valued for laboratory and industrial equipment such as reaction vessels and vacuum furnaces due to its chemical inertness and very high melting point. It is used in tantalum capacitors for electronic equipment such as computers. It is being investigated for use as a material for high-quality superconducting resonators in quantum processors.
73.characteristics: Tantalum is dark blue-gray, dense, ductile, very hard, and highly conductive of heat and electricity. It has a melting point of 3017 °C, exceeded only by tungsten, rhenium, osmium, and carbon among elements. Below 150 °C it is almost completely immune to attack by aqua regia, though it can be dissolved by hydrofluoric acid and other specific acidic solutions.

74.name: tungsten
74.description: Tungsten is a chemical element with symbol W and atomic number 74, a metal found naturally on Earth almost exclusively in compounds with other elements. It was identified as a distinct element in 1781 and first isolated as a metal in 1783. Its important ores include scheelite and wolframite.
74.uses: Tungsten occurs in many alloys with numerous applications including incandescent light bulb filaments, X-ray tubes, electrodes in gas tungsten arc welding, superalloys, and radiation shielding. Its largest use is in tungsten carbide, a wear-resistant material used in metalworking, mining, and construction. Tungsten compounds are used as industrial catalysts and its hardness and high density make it suitable for military applications in penetrating projectiles.
74.characteristics: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all known elements at 3,422 °C and the highest boiling point at 5,930 °C, with a density of 19.254 g/cm³. Polycrystalline tungsten is an intrinsically brittle and hard material, though pure single-crystalline tungsten is more ductile. It is a mostly non-reactive element that does not react with water, most acids and bases, or oxygen at room temperature, but reacts directly with fluorine at room temperature.

75.name: rhenium
75.description: Rhenium is a silvery-gray, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table with atomic number 75. With an estimated average concentration of 1 part per billion, it is one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust. It has one of the highest melting and boiling points of any element and can assume oxidation states ranging from −3 to +7.
75.uses: Nickel-based superalloys of rhenium are used in combustion chambers, turbine blades, and exhaust nozzles of jet engines, making jet engine construction the largest single use for the element. The second-most important use is as a catalyst, where it is excellent for hydrogenation and isomerization, particularly in catalytic reforming of naphtha for use in gasoline through the rheniforming process. Platinum-rhenium catalysts are also primarily used in making lead-free, high-octane gasoline.
75.characteristics: Rhenium is a silvery-white metal with one of the highest melting points of all elements, exceeded only by tungsten, and has one of the highest boiling points among stable elements. It is also one of the densest elements, exceeded only by platinum, iridium, and osmium, with a hexagonal close-packed crystal structure. When annealed, it is very ductile and can be bent, coiled, or rolled, and it resists alkalis and common acids at room temperature and atmospheric pressure.

76.name: osmium
76.description: Osmium is a hard, brittle, bluish-white transition metal in the platinum group with the highest density of any stable element. It is a chemical element with symbol Os and atomic number 76, and has one of the lowest abundances in the Earth's crust.
76.uses: Manufacturers use alloys of osmium with platinum, iridium, and other platinum-group metals for fountain pen nib tipping, electrical contacts, and other applications that require extreme durability and hardness. Osmium was also an early successful catalyst in the Haber process for nitrogen fixation.
76.characteristics: Osmium is a hard, brittle, blue-gray metal that is about twice as dense as lead, with a density of 22.587 g/cm³ at 20 °C. It has very high hardness at 4 GPa and an extremely high bulk modulus between 395 and 462 GPa, rivaling diamond. The metal has a very low vapor pressure and the fourth highest melting point of all elements, remains lustrous at high temperatures, and forms compounds with oxidation states ranging from −2 to +8.

77.name: iridium
77.description: Iridium is a chemical element with symbol Ir and atomic number 77. It is a very hard, brittle, silvery-white transition metal of the platinum group, considered the second-densest naturally occurring metal after osmium with a density of 22.56 g/cm³. It is one of the most corrosion-resistant metals, remaining resistant even at temperatures as high as 2,000 °C.
77.uses: The dominant uses of iridium and its alloys are in high-performance spark plugs, crucibles for recrystallization of semiconductors at high temperatures, and electrodes for the production of chlorine in the chloralkali process. Important compounds of iridium are chlorides and iodides in industrial catalysis, and iridium is a component of some OLEDs. The radioisotope iridium-192 finds application in brachytherapy and industrial radiography for nondestructive testing of welds.
77.characteristics: Iridium is white with a slight yellowish cast, extremely brittle and hard, with a very high melting point and the 10th highest boiling point among all elements. It is the only metal to maintain good mechanical properties in air at temperatures above 1,600 °C and becomes a superconductor below 0.14 K. Iridium has the second-highest modulus of elasticity among metals and is the most corrosion-resistant metal known, not attacked by acids including aqua regia.

78.name: platinum
78.description: Platinum is a dense, malleable, ductile, highly unreactive, precious, silverish-white transition metal with atomic number 78 and symbol Pt. It is a member of the platinum group of elements and group 10 of the periodic table, with six naturally occurring isotopes. One of the rarer elements in Earth's crust with an average abundance of approximately 5 μg/kg, it is highly valuable as a major precious metal commodity.
78.uses: Platinum is a key component in catalytic converters, laboratory equipment, electrical contacts and electrodes, platinum resistance thermometers, dentistry equipment, and jewelry. It is used in the glass industry to manipulate molten glass, and platinum compounds such as cisplatin, oxaliplatin and carboplatin are applied in chemotherapy as treatment for certain types of cancer. Hexachloroplatinic acid serves as a precursor for many platinum compounds and has applications in photography, zinc etchings, indelible ink, plating, mirrors, and porcelain coloring.
78.characteristics: Platinum is lustrous, ductile, and malleable, being the most ductile of pure metals and more ductile than gold, silver or copper. It does not corrode and bulk platinum does not oxidize in air at any temperature, making it a noble metal. Its most common oxidation states are +2 and +4, and although generally unreactive, it is attacked by chlorine, bromine, iodine, sulfur, and fluorine, and dissolves in hot aqua regia.

79.name: gold
79.description: Gold is a chemical element with atomic number 79 and symbol Au. In its pure form, it is a bright metallic-yellow, dense, soft, malleable, and ductile metal that is a transition metal and one of the noble metals, ranking second lowest in the reactivity series with only platinum being less reactive.
79.uses: Gold has been used for coinage, jewelry, and works of art throughout recorded history. Its chief industrial use is in corrosion-resistant electrical connectors in computerized devices due to its conductivity and resistance to corrosion, and it is also used in infrared shielding, colored glass production, gold leafing, tooth restoration, and in the drug auranofin for treating rheumatoid arthritis.
79.characteristics: Gold is the most malleable metal and can be beaten into extremely thin sheets or drawn into single-atom-width wires without noticeable hardening. It has a density of 19.3 g/cm³, is a good conductor of heat and electricity, and possesses a distinctive reddish-yellow color due to relativistic quantum chemical effects. Gold is resistant to most acids except aqua regia and dissolves in alkaline cyanide solutions and mercury, and it does not react with oxygen at any temperature.

80.name: mercury
80.description: Mercury is a chemical element with symbol Hg and atomic number 80, commonly known as quicksilver. It is a heavy, silvery d-block metal and the only metallic element that is liquid at standard temperature and pressure. It has the lowest freezing point, lowest boiling point, and narrowest liquid state range of any metal under standard conditions.
80.uses: Mercury is used in thermometers, barometers, manometers, sphygmomanometers, float valves, mercury switches, mercury relays, and fluorescent lamps, though its use has been reduced due to toxicity concerns. It remains in use in scientific research applications and in amalgam for dental restoration in some locales, and is still used in fluorescent lighting where electricity passed through mercury vapor produces ultraviolet light that causes phosphor to fluoresce.
80.characteristics: Mercury is a heavy, silvery-white metal that is liquid at standard conditions with a melting point of −38.83 °C and boiling point of 356.73 °C. Compared to other metals, it is a poor conductor of heat but a fair conductor of electricity, and was the first known superconductor discovered in 1911. Mercury readily dissolves many metals such as gold and silver to form amalgams, though iron is resistant to amalgam formation.

81.name: thallium
81.description: Thallium is a silvery-white post-transition metal with atomic number 81 that is not found free in nature. When isolated, it resembles tin but discolors when exposed to air. It was discovered independently by William Crookes and Claude-Auguste Lamy in 1861 using flame spectroscopy, and the name derives from the Greek word for "green shoot" due to its characteristic green spectral line.
81.uses: Approximately 65% of thallium production is used in the electronics industry, with the remainder used in the pharmaceutical industry and glass manufacturing. It is also used in infrared detectors. The radioisotope thallium-201 is used in small amounts in nuclear medicine scans during cardiac stress tests. Soluble thallium salts were historically used in rat poisons and insecticides, though these uses have been restricted or banned in many countries due to toxicity.
81.characteristics: Thallium is a soft, highly electrically conducting metal with a low melting point of 304°C and is malleable and sectile enough to be cut with a knife. It has a metallic luster that quickly tarnishes to a bluish-gray tinge when exposed to air, and a heavy layer of oxide builds up on the metal if left in air. Thallium reacts with water to form thallium hydroxide and tends to form +3 and +1 oxidation states, with the +1 state being far more prominent in thallium than in other group 13 elements.

82.name: lead
82.description: A heavy metal chemical element with atomic number 82 and symbol Pb, characterized by its soft, malleable nature and relatively low melting point. It appears shiny silvery with a bluish tint when freshly cut or melted, but tarnishes to dull gray on exposure to air. Lead is the highest atomic number of any stable element, with three of its isotopes serving as endpoints of major nuclear decay chains.
82.uses: Lead has been extensively used since ancient times in construction, plumbing, batteries, bullets, shots, weights, solders, pewter, fusible alloys, lead paints, leaded gasoline, and radiation shielding. It played a crucial role in the development of the printing press, as movable type could be relatively easily cast from lead alloys. In 2022, about twelve million tonnes of lead were produced globally, with two-thirds coming from recycling.
82.characteristics: Lead is characterized by high density (11.34 g/cm³), malleability, ductility, and resistance to corrosion due to passivation. It is soft with a Mohs hardness of 1.5 and melts at 327.5 °C, making it one of the lowest melting points among metals. It becomes a superconductor below 7.19 K and is a neurotoxin that accumulates in soft tissues and bones, damaging the nervous system and interfering with biological enzymes.

83.name: bismuth
83.description: Bismuth is a chemical element with symbol Bi and atomic number 83. It is a post-transition metal and one of the pnictogens, with chemical properties resembling arsenic and antimony. Elemental bismuth occurs naturally, and its sulfide and oxide forms are important commercial ores.
83.uses: Bismuth compounds are used in cosmetics, pigments, and pharmaceuticals such as bismuth subsalicylate for treating diarrhea. Its unusual expansion upon solidification made it useful in casting printing type, and suitable bismuth alloys have gained popularity as replacements for lead in various applications.
83.characteristics: Bismuth is a brittle metal with a silvery-white color that develops a rosy cast from surface oxidation and can display iridescent colors from thin-film interference. It is the most diamagnetic element, has among the highest electrical resistivity and lowest thermal conductivity of all metals, and expands 3.32% upon solidification. It has unusually low toxicity for a heavy metal and was long regarded as the heaviest stable nuclide before being found slightly radioactive in 2003.

84.name: polonium
84.description: Polonium is a rare and highly radioactive metal with no stable isotopes, classified as a chalcogen chemically similar to selenium and tellurium, though its metallic character resembles thallium, lead, and bismuth. It has symbol Po and atomic number 84, with all 42 known isotopes being radioactive. Due to the short half-life of all its isotopes, its natural occurrence is limited to tiny traces, primarily polonium-210 in uranium ores.
84.uses: Polonium has few applications, all related to its radioactivity: heaters in space probes, antistatic devices, sources of neutrons and alpha particles, and as a poison. It was also used as a key ingredient in the 'Urchin' initiator at the center of nuclear bomb pits during the Manhattan Project.
84.characteristics: Polonium exists in two metallic allotropes, with the alpha form being a simple cubic crystal structure at standard temperature and pressure. Polonium-210 is an alpha emitter with a half-life of 138.4 days and is 5,000 times more radioactive than radium; it becomes airborne with ease, with 50% vaporization occurring at 55°C in 45 hours, despite having a melting point of 254°C and boiling point of 962°C. Polonium dissolves readily in dilute acids and its solutions change from pink to yellow due to alpha radiation ionizing the solvent and converting Po2+ into Po4+.

85.name: astatine
85.description: Astatine is a chemical element with symbol At and atomic number 85. It is the rarest naturally occurring element in the Earth's crust, occurring only as the decay product of heavier elements. All of astatine's isotopes are short-lived, with the most stable being astatine-210 with a half-life of 8.1 hours.
85.uses: Astatine-211 is medically useful and astatine is capable of acting as a metal in antibody radiolabeling. It has been studied for its various chemical properties and compounds, though practical applications are limited by its extreme radioactivity and short half-life.
85.characteristics: Astatine is extremely radioactive with all isotopes having half-lives of 8.1 hours or less. It is likely to have a dark or lustrous appearance and may be a semiconductor or possibly a metal. Chemically, it displays both nonmetallic characteristics similar to iodine and some metallic behavior similar to silver, with an electronegativity of 2.2 on the revised Pauling scale.

86.name: radon
86.description: Radon is a chemical element with symbol Rn and atomic number 86. It is a radioactive noble gas that is colorless, odorless, and tasteless. Of the three naturally occurring radon isotopes, only 222Rn has a sufficiently long half-life of 3.825 days to be released from soil and rock where it is generated.
86.uses: Radon can be used as a natural tracer in physical sciences due to its 3.8-day half-life. Techniques such as sub-slab depressurization are used for radon mitigation in buildings. Radon compounds have been considered for radon gas removal in uranium mines.
86.characteristics: Radon is the densest of the noble gases with a density of 9.73 kg/m³ at standard temperature and pressure, about 8 times denser than Earth's atmosphere. It forms a monatomic gas and is colorless at standard conditions; when cooled below its boiling point of 211.5 K, concentrated liquid radon emits radioluminescence of varying color. Radon is chemically inert to most common reactions due to its eight electrons in the outer valence shell, though it is more reactive than xenon and can form compounds with powerful oxidizing agents such as fluorine.

87.name: francium
87.description: Francium is a chemical element with symbol Fr and atomic number 87. It is extremely radioactive with its most stable isotope francium-223 having a half-life of only 22 minutes. It is the second-most electropositive element behind caesium and classed as an alkali metal.
87.uses: Due to its extreme instability and rarity, francium has no commercial applications. It has been used for research purposes in chemistry and atomic structure, particularly in specialized spectroscopy experiments that have provided data on atomic energy levels. Its use as a potential diagnostic aid for various cancers has been explored but deemed impractical, and it is a prospective candidate for searching for CP violation.
87.characteristics: Francium is one of the most unstable naturally occurring elements and as an alkali metal with a single valence electron, its chemical properties mostly resemble those of caesium. Its estimated melting point is around 8–27 °C with an estimated boiling point of 620 °C, though these values are uncertain due to the element's extreme rarity and radioactivity. Its density is expected to be around 2.48 g/cm³ and it has an estimated electronegativity of 0.7 on the Pauling scale.

88.name: radium
88.description: Radium is a chemical element with symbol Ra and atomic number 88, the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table known as the alkaline earth metals. It is the heaviest known alkaline earth metal and the only radioactive member of its group. Pure radium is a volatile, lustrous silvery-white metal that readily reacts with nitrogen upon exposure to air, forming a black surface layer of radium nitride.
88.uses: Radium was widely used in self-luminous paints following its discovery due to its property of emitting ionizing radiation that can excite fluorescent chemicals and cause radioluminescence. From the 1910s to the 1970s, it was used as a radioactive source for radioluminescent devices and in radioactive quackery for its supposed curative power. As of 2018, other than in nuclear medicine and the production of actinium in nuclear reactors, radium has no commercial applications, having been replaced with less dangerous radioisotopes in nearly all its applications.
88.characteristics: All isotopes of radium are radioactive, with radium-226 being the most stable with a half-life of 1,600 years. Radium has a melting point of either 700°C or 960°C and a boiling point of 1,737°C, with a density of 5.5 g/cm³. It crystallizes in a body-centered cubic structure and is considered particularly toxic and carcinogenic due to its radioactivity and its tendency to accumulate in bones by mimicking calcium.

89.name: actinium
89.description: A soft, silvery-white radioactive metal with symbol Ac and atomic number 89. It was discovered by André-Louis Debierne in 1899, and the actinide series of 15 elements is named after actinium.
89.uses: Its current applications include use as a neutron source and an agent for radiation therapy. It has no significant industrial use due to its scarcity, high price, and radioactivity.
89.characteristics: Actinium reacts rapidly with oxygen and moisture in air, forming a white coating of actinium oxide that prevents further oxidation. It assumes oxidation state +3 in nearly all its chemical compounds and glows in the dark with a pale blue light due to its strong radioactivity. The naturally occurring isotope 227Ac decays with a half-life of 21.772 years, predominantly emitting beta particles and sometimes alpha particles.

90.name: thorium
90.description: Thorium is a weakly radioactive light silver metal with atomic number 90 that tarnishes olive grey when exposed to air. It is moderately soft, malleable, and has a high melting point of 1750 °C. As an electropositive actinide, its chemistry is dominated by the +4 oxidation state and it is quite reactive, capable of igniting in air when finely divided.
90.uses: Thorium is used as an alloying element in TIG welding electrodes and in strengthening magnesium. It has been used in high-end optics, scientific instrumentation, broadcast vacuum tubes, and as the light source in gas mantles, though these uses have become marginal. It is also used in coating tungsten wire, controlling grain size in electric lamps, high-temperature crucibles, glasses for lenses, heat-resistant ceramics, aircraft engines, and light bulbs, and ocean science uses thorium isotope ratios to understand ancient oceans.
90.characteristics: Thorium is a moderately soft, paramagnetic, bright silvery metal that is very ductile and can be cold-rolled, swaged, and drawn. At room temperature it has a face-centred cubic crystal structure with a bulk modulus of 54 GPa and becomes superconductive below 1.4 K. It has a density of approximately 11.5 to 11.66 g/cm³ and is nearly half as dense as uranium and plutonium while being harder than both.

91.name: protactinium
91.description: Protactinium is a dense, radioactive, silvery-gray actinide metal with atomic number 91 and symbol Pa. It readily reacts with oxygen, water vapor, and inorganic acids, and forms various chemical compounds where it is usually present in the oxidation state +5, though it can also assume +4, +3, or +2 states. It is one of the rarest and most expensive naturally occurring elements, with concentrations in the Earth's crust typically a few parts per trillion, but reaching up to a few parts per million in some uraninite ore deposits.
91.uses: Because of its scarcity, high radioactivity, and high toxicity, there are currently no uses for protactinium outside scientific research. In ocean science, analysis of the relative concentrations of various uranium, thorium, and protactinium isotopes in water and minerals is used in radiometric dating of sediments up to 175,000 years old and in modeling of various geological processes. Protactinium-233 is produced as an intermediate product in thorium-based nuclear reactors for the production of the fissile uranium-233.
91.characteristics: Protactinium is an actinide metal that is highly radioactive and toxic. It has naturally occurring isotopes 231Pa and 234Pa, with 231Pa being nearly all natural protactinium and having a half-life of 32,760 years as an alpha emitter. Thirty radioisotopes of protactinium have been discovered, ranging from 210Pa to 239Pa, with most having half-lives shorter than 1.6 days.

92.name: uranium
92.description: Uranium is a silvery-grey metal in the actinide series with atomic number 92. It is radioactive and has the highest atomic weight of naturally occurring elements, with a density about 70% higher than lead. It occurs naturally in low concentrations in soil, rock, and water.
92.uses: Uranium is used in nuclear power plants and nuclear weapons because uranium-235 is the only naturally occurring fissile element present in significant amounts. Civilian applications include fueling nuclear reactors to produce electricity, and historical uses include colorants for glass and pottery glazes. Depleted uranium is used in kinetic energy penetrators, armor plating, shielding materials, and as counterweights in aircraft.
92.characteristics: Uranium is a silvery white, weakly radioactive metal with a Mohs hardness of 6, sufficient to scratch glass. It is malleable, ductile, slightly paramagnetic, and a poor electrical conductor with a very high density of 19.1 g/cm³. It reacts with almost all non-metallic elements except noble gases, and its reactivity increases with temperature.

93.name: neptunium
93.description: Neptunium is a radioactive actinide metal with atomic number 93, representing the first transuranic element. It is named after Neptune, the planet beyond Uranus in the Solar System. A neptunium atom has 93 protons and 93 electrons, with seven valence electrons.
93.uses: Neptunium is used as a precursor for the formation of plutonium-238, which is employed in radioisotope thermal generators to provide electricity for spacecraft. It has also been used in detectors of high-energy neutrons.
93.characteristics: Neptunium metal is silvery and tarnishes when exposed to air, forming a thin oxide layer. The element is hard, ductile, and radioactive, with a melting point of 639 ± 3 °C and exhibits five oxidation states ranging from +3 to +7. Like all actinides, it is poisonous, pyrophoric, and capable of accumulating in bones, occurring in at least three allotropic forms.

94.name: plutonium
94.description: Plutonium is a silvery-gray actinide metal with atomic number 94 that tarnishes when exposed to air and forms a dull coating when oxidized. It normally exhibits six allotropes and four oxidation states, and reacts with carbon, halogens, nitrogen, silicon, and hydrogen. The element is radioactive and was first synthesized in 1940-1941 by deuteron bombardment of uranium-238 at the University of California, Berkeley.
94.uses: Plutonium-239 and plutonium-241 are fissile isotopes used in nuclear weapons and nuclear reactors. Plutonium-238, with a half-life of 87.7 years, is used as a heat source in radioisotope thermoelectric generators that power some spacecraft. Plutonium oxides are preferred for applications such as nuclear fission reactor fuel.
94.characteristics: At room temperature, plutonium has a silvery appearance but oxidizes quickly to dull gray, though yellow and olive green are also reported. It has a low melting point of 640 °C and an unusually high boiling point of 3,228 °C. Unlike most metals, plutonium is not a good conductor of heat or electricity, and it increases in density by 2.5% when it melts, which is unusual behavior for a metal.

95.name: americium
95.description: Americium is a synthetic radioactive chemical element with atomic number 95 and symbol Am. It is a transuranic member of the actinide series in the periodic table, located under the lanthanide element europium, and was named after the Americas by analogy.
95.uses: Americium is widely used in commercial ionization chamber smoke detectors, as well as in neutron sources and industrial gauges. Several unusual applications have been proposed for the isotope 242mAm, such as nuclear batteries or fuel for space ships with nuclear propulsion, though these remain hindered by scarcity and high cost.
95.characteristics: Americium is a relatively soft radioactive metal with a silvery appearance. Its most common isotopes are 241Am and 243Am, and in chemical compounds it usually assumes the oxidation state +3. The crystal lattices of solid americium contain small intrinsic radiogenic defects due to self-irradiation with alpha particles, which accumulate over time and can cause property drift, particularly in older samples.

96.name: curium
96.description: Curium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Cm and atomic number 96. It is a transuranic actinide element named after Marie and Pierre Curie for their research on radioactivity. It was first intentionally synthesized in 1944 by Glenn T. Seaborg, Ralph A. James, and Albert Ghiorso using a cyclotron at Berkeley by bombarding plutonium-239 with alpha particles.
96.uses: Curium is used in making heavier actinides and the 238Pu radionuclide for power sources in artificial cardiac pacemakers and radioisotope thermoelectric generators for spacecraft. It served as the alpha-source in alpha particle X-ray spectrometers on several space probes, including the Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity Mars rovers and the Philae lander, to analyze the composition and structure of surfaces.
96.characteristics: Curium is a hard, dense, silvery metal with a melting point of 1344°C and boiling point of 3556°C, significantly higher than earlier actinides. It is paramagnetic at ambient conditions but becomes antiferromagnetic upon cooling to 65–52 K. In compounds, curium usually has valence +3 and sometimes +4, and it readily oxidizes with its oxides being a dominant form; it also forms strongly fluorescent complexes with organic compounds showing yellow-orange fluorescence at 590–640 nm.

97.name: berkelium
97.description: Berkelium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Bk and atomic number 97, a member of the actinide and transuranium element series. It was discovered in December 1949 at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in Berkeley, California, making it the fifth transuranium element discovered.
97.uses: Berkelium has no practical application outside scientific research, which is mostly directed at the synthesis of heavier transuranium elements and superheavy elements. For example, a sample of berkelium-249 was used to synthesize the new element tennessine for the first time in 2009.
97.characteristics: Berkelium is a soft, silvery-white, radioactive metal with a density of 14.78 g/cm³ and a melting point of 986 °C. The berkelium-249 isotope emits low-energy beta particles and decays with a half-life of 330 days to californium-249. It exhibits paramagnetic behavior between 70 K and room temperature with an effective magnetic moment of 9.69 Bohr magnetons, and undergoes a transition to an antiferromagnetic state upon cooling to about 34 K.

98.name: californium
98.description: Californium is a synthetic actinide element with symbol Cf and atomic number 98, first synthesized in 1950 at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory by bombarding curium with alpha particles. It is a silvery-white metal that is the sixth transuranium element to be synthesized and has the second-highest atomic mass of all elements produced in visible quantities.
98.uses: Californium has practical applications as a neutron source, including helping to start up nuclear reactors, studying materials through neutron diffraction and neutron spectroscopy, treating certain cervical and brain cancers, conducting neutron activation analysis, and synthesizing higher mass elements. Certain isotopes of californium, particularly 252Cf, are used for these purposes because they emit neutrons.
98.characteristics: Californium is a malleable metal with a melting point of 900 ± 30 °C and an estimated boiling point of 1,743 K. It exhibits oxidation states of 4, 3, or 2, with the +3 state being dominant, and slowly tarnishes in air at room temperature. The element has two crystalline forms at standard pressure: an alpha form below 600–800 °C with density of 15.10 g/cm3 and a beta form above 600–800 °C with density of 8.74 g/cm3.

99.name: einsteinium
99.description: Einsteinium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Es and atomic number 99, and is a member of the actinide series and the seventh transuranium element. It is a soft, silvery, paramagnetic metal whose chemistry is typical of the late actinides with a preponderance of the +3 oxidation state. It was discovered in 1952 as a component of the debris from the first hydrogen bomb explosion.
99.uses: Due to the small amounts of einsteinium produced and the short half-life of its most common isotope, there are no practical applications for it except basic scientific research. Einsteinium was used to synthesize, for the first time, 17 atoms of the new element mendelevium in 1955.
99.characteristics: Einsteinium is a soft, silvery, paramagnetic metal with a density of 8.84 g/cm³ and a melting point of 860 °C. The high radioactivity of einsteinium-253 produces a visible glow and rapidly damages its crystalline metal lattice, with released heat of about 1,000 watts per gram. Like all synthetic transuranium elements, isotopes of einsteinium are very radioactive and are considered highly dangerous to health on ingestion.

100.name: fermium
100.description: Fermium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Fm and atomic number 100. It is an actinide and the heaviest element that can be formed by neutron bombardment of lighter elements, representing the last element that can be prepared in macroscopic quantities, though pure fermium metal has not yet been prepared.
100.uses: Owing to the small amounts of produced fermium and all of its isotopes having relatively short half-lives, there are currently no uses for it outside basic scientific research.
100.characteristics: Fermium's chemistry is typical for the late actinides, with a preponderance of the +3 oxidation state but also an accessible +2 oxidation state. A total of 20 isotopes are known, with 257Fm being the longest-lived with a half-life of 100.5 days, while other isotopes have considerably shorter half-lives.

101.name: mendelevium
101.description: Mendelevium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Md and atomic number 101. It is a metallic radioactive transuranium element in the actinide series and the first element by atomic number that currently cannot be produced in macroscopic quantities by neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It is the thirteenth actinide, the ninth transuranic element, and the first transfermium, named after Dmitri Mendeleev, the father of the periodic table.
101.uses: There are currently no uses for mendelevium outside basic scientific research, as only small amounts are produced.
101.characteristics: Mendelevium has a dominant +3 oxidation state but also a +2 oxidation state accessible in solution, with a +1 state also reported but not yet confirmed. All known isotopes have short half-lives. Mendelevium metal has not been prepared in bulk and is predicted to be divalent with a metallic radius around 194±10 pm, a melting point estimated at 800°C, and density around 10.3±0.7 g/cm³.

102.name: nobelium
102.description: Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol No and atomic number 102, named after Alfred Nobel. It is a radioactive metal that is the tenth transuranium element, the second transfermium, and the fourteenth member of the actinide series. It can only be produced in particle accelerators by bombarding lighter elements with charged particles.
102.uses: Nobelium is used in chemistry experiments to study the behavior of heavier homologs in the periodic table. The isotope 255No is most commonly used in chemistry because it can be produced on a larger scale, despite shorter-lived isotopes existing.
102.characteristics: Nobelium is a radioactive metal with twelve known isotopes; the most stable is 259No with a half-life of 58 minutes. It behaves as a heavier homolog to ytterbium and exhibits a stable +2 oxidation state in aqueous solution, which is much more stable than the +3 state characteristic of other actinides. Nobelium metal has not yet been prepared in bulk quantities, and bulk preparation is currently impossible.

103.name: lawrencium
103.description: Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Lr and atomic number 103, named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron. It is a radioactive metal that represents the eleventh transuranium element, the third transfermium, and the last member of the actinide series. Like all elements with atomic number over 100, it can only be produced in particle accelerators by bombarding lighter elements with charged particles.
103.uses: Lawrencium is most commonly used in chemistry through its isotope 260Lr, which has a half-life of 2.7 minutes and can be produced on a larger scale than the more stable 266Lr isotope. Chemistry experiments have been performed to study its behavior and chemical properties, including its reactions and ionic characteristics in aqueous solution.
103.characteristics: Lawrencium is expected to be a trivalent, silvery metal with a hexagonal close-packed crystal structure similar to lutetium. It has an estimated density of around 14.4 g/cm³, an estimated melting point around 1900 K (1600 °C), and a trivalent metallic radius of 171 pm. It is easily oxidized by air, steam, and acids, and chemically behaves as a heavier homolog to lutetium with an anomalous electron configuration of s2p instead of s2d.

104.name: rutherfordium
104.description: Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Rf and atomic number 104, named after physicist Ernest Rutherford. It is not found in nature and can only be made in a particle accelerator. It is a radioactive d-block element in period 7 and group 4, behaving as the heavier homolog to hafnium.
104.characteristics: The most stable known isotope, 267Rf, has a half-life of about 48 minutes. Rutherfordium is expected to form a very stable, refractory oxide (RfO2) and reacts with halogens to form volatile tetrahalides (RfX4). It exhibits a stable +4 oxidation state and is expected to form a less stable +3 state, with chemical properties resembling other group 4 elements rather than lead.

105.name: dubnium
105.description: Dubnium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Db and atomic number 105. It is highly radioactive, with the most stable known isotope, dubnium-268, having a half-life of about 16 hours. Dubnium does not occur naturally on Earth and is produced artificially.
105.characteristics: Dubnium is a member of group 5 in the 6d series of transition metals, placing it under vanadium, niobium, and tantalum. It should share most properties with the other group 5 elements, such as its valence electron configuration and a dominant +5 oxidation state, though with some anomalies due to relativistic effects. Limited investigation of dubnium chemistry has confirmed these theoretical predictions.

106.name: seaborgium
106.description: Seaborgium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Sg and atomic number 106, named after American nuclear chemist Glenn T. Seaborg. It is a d-block transactinide element belonging to group 6 as the fourth member of the 6d series of transition metals in the 7th period. As a synthetic element, it is created in laboratories but not found in nature and is radioactive with the most stable known isotopes having half-lives on the order of several minutes.
106.uses: Very few chemical reactions of seaborgium have been studied due to the difficulty of producing and isolating the element. A few inorganic compounds and a carbonyl believed to be Sg(CO)6 have been synthesized to investigate seaborgium's chemical properties.
106.characteristics: Seaborgium is radioactive with no stable or naturally occurring isotopes. Experiments have confirmed that seaborgium behaves as the heavier homologue to tungsten in group 6, and fourteen different radioactive isotopes with mass numbers 257–269 and 271 have been synthesized, all of which decay through alpha decay and spontaneous fission except seaborgium-261 which can also undergo electron capture.

107.name: bohrium
107.description: Bohrium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Bh and atomic number 107, named after Danish physicist Niels Bohr. As a synthetic element, it can only be created in particle accelerators and is not found in nature. In the periodic table, it is a transactinide element in the d-block, a member of the 7th period and group 7 elements as the fifth member of the 6d series of transition metals.
107.characteristics: All known isotopes of bohrium are highly radioactive; the most stable known isotope is 270Bh with a half-life of approximately 2.4 minutes. Chemistry experiments have confirmed that bohrium behaves as the heavier homologue to rhenium in group 7, with chemical properties that compare well with other group 7 elements. Bohrium is expected to be a solid under normal conditions with a hexagonal close-packed crystal structure and a predicted density of 26–27 g/cm³.

108.name: hassium
108.discoverer: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
108.description: Hassium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Hs and atomic number 108 that is highly radioactive, with its most stable known isotopes having half-lives of about ten seconds. It is a superheavy transactinide element and a member of period 7 and group 8, making it the sixth member of the 6d series of transition metals. Natural occurrences of hassium have been hypothesized but never found.
108.uses: Chemistry experiments have confirmed that hassium behaves as the heavier homologue to osmium, reacting readily with oxygen to form a volatile tetroxide.
108.characteristics: Hassium is highly radioactive with most stable known isotopes having half-lives of about ten seconds. One of its isotopes, 270Hs, has magic numbers of protons and neutrons for deformed nuclei, giving it greater stability against spontaneous fission. The chemical properties of hassium compare well with the chemistry of other group 8 elements.

109.name: meitnerium
109.discoverer: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
109.description: Meitnerium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Mt and atomic number 109. It is an extremely radioactive synthetic element not found in nature but created in laboratories. It is a d-block transactinide element in the 7th period and group 9 of the periodic table.
109.characteristics: The most stable known isotope, meitnerium-278, has a half-life of 4.5 seconds. It is expected to be a solid metal with a face-centered cubic crystal structure and a density of around 27-28 g/cm³, making it one of the heaviest known elements. Meitnerium is calculated to be paramagnetic and to have properties similar to its lighter homologues cobalt, rhodium, and iridium.

110.name: darmstadtium
110.discoverer: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
110.description: Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Ds and atomic number 110. It is a d-block transactinide element in the 7th period and group 10 of the periodic table. It is extremely radioactive, with the most stable known isotope, darmstadtium-281, having a half-life of approximately 14 seconds.
110.characteristics: Darmstadtium is calculated to have similar properties to its lighter homologues nickel, palladium, and platinum. It is expected to be a very noble metal and a very heavy solid with a density of around 26–27 g/cm³. Its outer electron configuration is calculated to be 6d8 7s2, and its atomic radius is expected to be around 132 pm.

111.name: roentgenium
111.discoverer: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
111.description: Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Rg and atomic number 111. It is extremely radioactive and can only be created in a laboratory. It is a d-block transactinide element and member of the 7th period, placed in group 11 elements.
111.uses: Roentgenium has no practical application. Only a few roentgenium atoms have ever been synthesized.
111.characteristics: The most stable known isotope, roentgenium-282, has a half-life of 100 seconds. Roentgenium is predicted to be a solid metal with a density around 22-24 g/cm³ and is calculated to have similar properties to its lighter homologues copper, silver, and gold, though it may show some differences from them.

112.name: copernicium
112.discoverer: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
112.description: Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Cn and atomic number 112. It is a d-block transactinide element and a group 12 element in the periodic table. All known isotopes are extremely radioactive and have only been created in laboratory settings.
112.uses: Copernicium has no practical uses due to its extreme radioactivity and the difficulty of synthesizing it. It is primarily studied for scientific research purposes, with its chemical properties being experimentally investigated as one of the heaviest elements in this regard.
112.characteristics: Copernicium is calculated to be an extremely volatile element, possibly a gas or volatile liquid at standard temperature and pressure. It is predicted to differ significantly from lighter group 12 elements due to relativistic effects, potentially showing the +4 oxidation state and having chemical similarities to noble gases. The most stable known isotope, copernicium-285, has a half-life of approximately 30 seconds.

113.name: nihonium
113.description: Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Nh and atomic number 113. It is extremely radioactive, with its most stable known isotope, nihonium-286, having a half-life of about 10 seconds. In the periodic table, it is a transactinide element in the p-block, belonging to period 7 and group 13.
113.characteristics: Nihonium has been calculated to have similar properties to boron, aluminium, gallium, indium, and thallium, and is expected to be a post-transition metal. It should be more stable in the +1 oxidation state than the +3 state, like thallium, but in the +1 state should behave more like silver and astatine. Preliminary experiments have shown that elemental nihonium is not very volatile and is less reactive than its lighter homologue thallium.

114.name: flerovium
114.description: Flerovium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Fl and atomic number 114. It is an extremely radioactive, superheavy transactinide element in the p-block of the periodic table, located in period 7 as the heaviest known member of the carbon group. Very little is known about flerovium since it can only be produced one atom at a time and all known isotopes are short-lived.
114.uses: The source text does not describe practical uses for flerovium.
114.characteristics: Flerovium is unexpectedly volatile for a group 14 element and shows very high volatility, possibly even gaseous at standard temperature and pressure, with behavior similar to copernicium in reactions with gold. It also appears to show some metallic properties consistent with it being the heavier homologue of lead. The most stable known isotope, 289Fl, has a half-life of approximately 2.1 seconds, with the unconfirmed 290Fl potentially having a longer half-life of 19 seconds.

115.name: moscovium
115.description: Moscovium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Mc and atomic number 115. It was first synthesized in 2003 by a joint team of Russian and American scientists at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia. It is a p-block transactinide element in the 7th period and group 15, making it the heaviest pnictogen.
115.characteristics: Moscovium is an extremely radioactive element with its most stable known isotope, moscovium-290, having a half-life of only 0.65 seconds. It is calculated to have properties similar to lighter pnictogens and to be a post-transition metal, with significant similarities to thallium. Chemical experimentation has confirmed that moscovium is less reactive than its lighter homologue bismuth.

116.name: livermorium
116.description: Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Lv and atomic number 116. It is an extremely radioactive element that has only been created in laboratories and has not been observed in nature. It is a p-block transactinide element in the 7th period, placed in group 16 as the heaviest chalcogen.
116.uses: No uses have been described in the source text.
116.characteristics: Livermorium is extremely radioactive with six known isotopes having mass numbers 288–293, with livermorium-293 being the longest-lived at about 80 milliseconds half-life. It is calculated to have some similar properties to lighter chalcogens like oxygen, sulfur, selenium, tellurium, and polonium, though it should show several major differences from them and is expected to be a post-transition metal.

117.name: tennessine
117.description: Tennessine is a synthetic element with symbol Ts and atomic number 117. It has the second-highest atomic number and joint-highest atomic mass of all known elements, and is the penultimate element of the 7th period of the periodic table. It is named after Tennessee, where key research institutions involved in its discovery are located.
117.characteristics: Tennessine is expected to be a member of group 17, the halogens, and is expected to be a volatile metal that neither forms anions nor achieves high oxidation states. The synthesized tennessine atoms have lasted tens and hundreds of milliseconds. Some of its properties may differ significantly from those of lighter halogens due to relativistic effects, though a few key properties such as melting and boiling points and first ionization energy are expected to follow the periodic trends of the halogens.

118.name: oganesson
118.description: Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element with symbol Og and atomic number 118. It is a p-block element and a member of group 18 on the periodic table of the elements, representing the last member of period 7. It has the highest atomic number and highest atomic mass of all known elements.
118.characteristics: Its only known isotope, oganesson-294, is highly radioactive with a half-life of 0.7 milliseconds. Theoretical studies predict that due to relativistic effects, it would be a solid at room temperature and significantly reactive, unlike the other noble gases. The element was first synthesized in 2002 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia.
